sites.name: A. Y. Mine
overview: On Leadville's Iron Hill, the A.Y. Mine helped launch the Guggenheim family's mining fortunes. After a difficult start with groundwater, rich silver-lead ore made the property important in the early 1880s. By the turn of the century, A.Y. was worked alongside the neighboring Minnie mine, shipping lead- and zinc-bearing ore and feeding a concentrating mill. Historic photographs and geological records document the A.Y. locality, but the mapped point is an approximate mine-area marker rather than a confirmed shaft opening. Nearby mine ruins are hazardous and may be on restricted property.
moreHistory: A.Y. Mine on Iron Hill was one of the important Leadville silver-lead properties associated with the Guggenheim family's entry into mining. A 2017 professional geological guide recounts Mayer Guggenheim's 1880 investment, water-pumping challenges and subsequent rich silver-lead discovery. An 1884 contemporary report names Graham and Guggenheim as partners after Samuel Harsh sold his share, with Thomas Weir taking over management. Federal geological reporting documented the mine's ore minerals, including galena, silver-bearing galena, sphalerite and secondary lead minerals. By 1888 A.Y. and neighboring Minnie were operated together under Weir. Contemporary 1900-1901 mining journals describe the combined A.Y. & Minnie operation shipping high-grade material and crude zinc/lead ores and treating roughly 100 tons of sulphide ore daily in its concentrating mill. A 1903 district review describes consolidation with A.M.W. and Mahala properties and expanded milling. USGS later listed the combined mill as operating in 1906. These combined-operation figures must not be attributed to the A.Y. shaft alone; nearby Minnie Pump Shaft and Colonel Sellers are separate scan targets.

sites.name: Adams Shaft
overview: On Yankee Hill above Leadville's Stray Horse Gulch, the Adams Shaft was part of the district's intense 1880s search for valuable ore. Mining reports from 1886 describe workers sinking toward deeper deposits, upgrading their hoisting equipment, and encountering chloride, galena, and carbonate mineralization. It belonged to the larger Adams Mining Company property, but was a separate working from the nearby Brookland and Keene shafts. A historical photograph held by the Lake County Public Library identifies the shaft in the gulch. The map marker shows an approximate historic location, not a verified surviving shaft entrance; do not enter old workings or cross private property.

timeline.text: Adams Mining Company organized to develop Leadville claims (company-level context).
Contemporary report locates Adams Shaft on Yankee Hill, near Keene Mine, while sinking toward the ore horizon.
Adams Shaft reported high-grade chloride ore; new hoisting and pumping equipment purchased.
Adams Shaft reported galena/carbonate mineralization; Brookland Shaft separately reported.
Adams Mining Company property leased to David H. Moffatt (company-wide, not shaft-specific).
Nicholson lease began, involving combined operation from the separate Wolftone shaft (company-wide).

moreHistory: Contemporary Engineering and Mining Journal accounts describe Adams Shaft on Yankee Hill, near the Keene workings, during active 1886 exploration. In March the shaft was being advanced toward a prospective ore horizon. In April miners reported a streak of high-grade chloride ore, prompting a new hoisting and pumping plant; the previous Adams hoist was slated for the distinct Brookland discovery shaft. In October the Adams shaft encountered galena and carbonate ore, reported at about 12 ounces silver per ton and 46.5% lead. The Adams Mining Company had been organized in 1883, and its wider Leadville holdings later passed through Moffatt and Nicholson leases, as described in a 1922 federal appellate opinion. Those company-wide leases, dividends, and later operations must not be represented as production or activity of this specific shaft. The Lake County Public Library preserves catalog metadata for a historic photograph depicting the Adams Shaft at Stray Horse Gulch; rights are restricted and the photograph has not been imported into the app.

sites.name: Adelaide Mine
overview: On Iron Hill, the Adelaide Mine became part of Leadville's early silver boom. Operators were building a smelter by 1878, but a fight over neighboring underground claims later reached the U.S. Supreme Court. In 1887 the justices upheld Adelaide's mining rights. This marker represents the approximate historic mine locality, not an identified shaft entrance.

timeline.text: Adelaide Lode located.
Operators erecting smelter.
U.S. Supreme Court affirms Adelaide claim rights.
Contemporary report describes ore chute through Adelaide.
EPA cultural survey identifies Adelaide (Ward).

moreHistory: Located 1876; in 1878 operators erected a smelter. A dispute with neighboring Argentine/Camp Bird over underground mining ground reached the U.S. Supreme Court, which affirmed Adelaide/Terrible Mining Company's rights in 1887. An 1892 mining journal described an ore chute extending through Adelaide property. EPA recorded Adelaide (Ward) as a contributing historic mining resource in 1997.

sites.name: Agwalt Tunnel
overview: Agwalt Tunnel was a large 1890s Leadville mining exploration project. In 1895 it had reached roughly 3,300 feet as miners sought ore associated with the nearby Little Johnny mine. The historic portal later collapsed, and the site received drainage cleanup in 1996. Its marker identifies an approximate historic locality.

timeline.text: Tunnel reported at 3,300 feet; company sought Little Johnny ore chute.
Agwalt company leased Tribune claim on Breece Hill.
EPA cleanup installed portal collection and drainage channels.

moreHistory: Contemporary reports in August and September 1895 describe Agwalt Mining Company led by Tingley S. Wood, a tunnel 3,300 feet long, plans to intersect the Little Johnny ore chute and a Tribune claim lease. USGS later mapped the tunnel. EPA recorded a collapsed portal and waste rock pile in Whites Gulch and installed drainage controls in 1996. No confirmed ore discovery or production total is established.

sites.name: Amity Shaft
overview: The Amity mine near Leadville was developed through several shafts beginning in the late nineteenth century. Its main shaft reached about 165 feet in 1907 and later connected to the Birdella tunnel. USGS historical research documents its production and underground workings.

timeline.text: Amity vein discovered.
Main shaft sunk to approximately 165 feet.
Birdella tunnel connected with Amity workings.
Reported intermittent ore production totaled 2,019 tons.
E. P. Chapman was working the mine and supplied historical information.

moreHistory: Amity vein discovered about 1887. Main shaft sunk to 165 ft in 1907. Birdella tunnel linked workings in 1916. USGS recorded 2,019 tons of intermittent ore output in 1915–39 and 1936 testimony from operator E. P. Chapman. MRDS manganese classification differs from USGS gold-silver production history.

sites.name: Ballard Mine
overview: On Leadville's Breece Hill, the Ballard Mine shipped gold-bearing ore in the late 1890s and drew attention for unusually bismuth-rich material. Contemporary accounts described a shaft reaching 450 feet by 1899. In 1902 the mine became the site of Leadville's first cyanide mill in its gold belt, an effort to recover gold from siliceous ore. The map marker identifies the historic mine locality, not an accessible shaft or mill ruin.

timeline.text: Contemporary Leadville mining reports described Ballard as an active ore shipper on Breece Hill; the shaft was reported at 450 feet deep, with ore extracted at the 415-foot level and bismuth-rich material shipped separately.

USGS historical compilation, quoting period reporting, identified James Golob of Ballard Mine as a promoter of the Golob-Colley Milling Company. The separate venture's planned feed from other mines must not be assigned to Ballard.
A cyanide mill was built at the Ballard Mine to treat siliceous gold ores; USGS characterized it as the first such mill in Leadville's gold belt.

moreHistory: Contemporary reporting in The Engineering and Mining Journal (21 October 1899) describes Ballard's newly opened ore bodies, daily shipments reportedly around 30 tons, a shaft 450 feet deep, and mining at the 415-foot level. Its ores contained gold, silver, lead and notable bismuth; some bismuth-rich ore was shipped to London brokers. A USGS historical compilation identifies Ballard among Breece Hill's heavy ore shippers in 1899 and names James Golob as associated with Ballard in a separate milling venture. In 1902, a cyanide mill was erected at the Ballard Mine to treat siliceous gold ores; the USGS called it the first cyanide mill in Leadville's gold belt. A modern USGS study independently identifies Ballard among Breece Hill's bismuth-bearing gold deposits, but regional production totals must not be attributed solely to Ballard.

sites.name: Ben Burb Shaft
overview: On Rock Hill near Leadville, the Ben Burb mine followed rich lead-bearing mineralization during the district's mining era. Records from 1883 describe its carbonate-of-lead ore; in 1905 miners deepened its shaft and drove toward the nearby Great O'Sullivan workings. That October, a mining journal reported a fresh ore discovery and shipments of about 20 tons per day. The mapped location is approximate and does not identify a safe or accessible shaft entrance.

timeline.text: Ben Burb reported producing carbonate-of-lead ore as part of Robert Emmet Consolidation.
March: shaft sinking underway, with drifting planned after completion.
July–September: a drift was driven toward the Great O'Sullivan workings.
October: a new lead-carbonate ore body was reported; contemporary shipments estimated at about 20 tons per day.

moreHistory: An 1883 mining trade-journal report described the Ben Burb mine of the Robert Emmet Consolidation working carbonate-of-lead ore on the same productive contact as neighboring Oro City. By March 1905 operators were sinking the Ben Burb shaft, located about 900 feet north of the Reindeer mine, planning to drift at depth. In July 1905 the journal described a drift from Ben Burb toward the Great O'Sullivan mine, intended to intersect ore and reach workings inaccessible through the older, water-affected O'Sullivan shaft; J. W. Weir held leases on both. September reporting described progress on the drift. In October 1905 the mine reportedly opened another lead-carbonate orebody and was shipping roughly 20 tons per day at that time. These are period reports rather than audited production totals.

sites.name: Bessie Wilgus Shaft
overview: Bessie Wilgus Shaft on Rock Hill reached over 400 feet by late 1904. Miners explored deeper limestone, developed underground workings and made a ventilation connection to nearby Reindeer. By 1907 it was shipping ore, with plans for further deepening. The mapped point is approximate and does not identify a safe entrance.

timeline.text: Shaft exceeded 400 feet.
Drifting and raising.
Ventilation connection to Reindeer.
Ore shipments and proposed deepening.

moreHistory: In 1904 the shaft reached over 400 feet in blue limestone. Prospecting in 1905 involved drifting and raising. In 1906 work paused for a ventilation connection to Reindeer. In 1907 the mine was reported shipping ore regularly and contracted to deepen 300 feet toward 800 feet; completion not verified. USGS 1926 related its ore bodies to down-faulted Rock Hill deposits. Reindeer and Sequin are separate mines.

sites.name: Big Pittsburg Mine
overview: On Fryer Hill above Leadville, Big Pittsburg was part of an ambitious effort to connect and develop neighboring silver-lead claims in the early 1880s. The company assembled several properties and worked multiple shafts as miners chased ore beneath the hill. Contemporary accounts record damaged old shafts, new drifts and silver-bearing ore discoveries, followed by leases that brought additional crews into the workings. Historic geologists mapped the ore zone passing through Big Pittsburg and adjacent Hibernia. The map marker shows an approximate historic mine locality, not an identified open shaft or safe visitor entrance.

timeline.text: February: Big Pittsburg Consolidated Mining Company was reported to combine the Big Pittsburg, Joe Bates, Gambetta, Gray Horse, and Ida Nyce properties at the base of Fryer Hill.
July: Mining-journal reports describe work at the Keene and McCormick shafts on or associated with the Big Pittsburg property, alongside replacement of unsafe or collapsed shafts.
August: Period reports describe the Pierson-to-Joe Bates development and discoveries of iron-rich ore carrying silver chlorides within the consolidated ground.
December: The company leased portions of its ground, including the Heystrosser and Joe Bates shaft areas; reports noted limited ore recovery from some leased workings.
A contemporary geological account traced the northern Fryer Hill ore chute through the north end of Big Pittsburg and Hibernia, while treating nearby mines as distinct.

moreHistory: In February 1880 a contemporary mining journal reported the creation of the Big Pittsburg Consolidated Mining Company through the grouping of Big Pittsburg with Joe Bates, Gambetta, Gray Horse and Ida Nyce properties near the base of Fryer Hill; the reported consideration in deeds was $323,000, though this was for the grouped properties, not a documented production value. July reports describe active shaft development, including Keene on the Big Pittsburg claim, McCormick near Hibernia, and replacement of unsafe or caved-in shafts elsewhere in the consolidated ground. By late August, reports described a drift at a 160-foot level toward the Bates workings intersecting iron-rich ore carrying silver chlorides. In December 1881 the company was leasing several parts of its holdings; the Heystrosser and Joe Bates shaft areas and ground leased to the Stonewall Jackson owners were discussed separately. An 1886 technical account traced the northern Fryer Hill ore chute through the north end of Big Pittsburg and Hibernia, demonstrating the geological relationship without making the two mines identical. Later USGS historical reporting described additional workings on the northern Big Pittsburg ground reached through Stonewall Jackson and a new shaft developed by other lessees. Precise shaft collars, total lifetime production, and surviving features are not established by these sources.

sites.name: Bison Shaft
overview: The Bison Shaft reveals why mining under Leadville could be both rewarding and exceptionally difficult. Underground miners cut through a maze of faults and porphyry intrusions; some of those same fractures helped concentrate valuable ore. A 1907 U.S. Geological Survey report describes the shaft's first level, the Bison and Pendery faults, and later tunnels that found rich ore beyond the fault. Its location is mapped approximately in the historic Downtown district. The scan point marks the historic mine locality, not a confirmed surviving shaft opening.
moreHistory: The Bison Shaft was an underground working in Leadville's Downtown mining district, east of the Pendery workings. In their 1907 USGS Bulletin 320, geologists Samuel Franklin Emmons and John Duer Irving gave the shaft its own detailed description (pp. 50–51). They described a particularly challenging zone of faults and branching sheets of Gray porphyry. Although the broken rock made mining and geological interpretation difficult, the same faults promoted secondary ore enrichment and rich discoveries. The shaft crossed a normal fault, named the Bison fault, just above its first level. Another small reverse fault lay east of the shaft, while the main Pendery fault lay at the end of an eastward drift, where contrasting quartzite and limestone formations met. The investigators also described duplicated Gray porphyry east of the shaft and later lower-level drifts that crossed the Bison fault westward to find large valuable ore bodies, mainly in limestone below White porphyry. The report emphasized that Bison had been worked intermittently by different operators and that incomplete records limited a complete reconstruction. The nearby Niles-Augusta mine is discussed as a separate working, not part of the Bison shaft. The MRDS-derived record categorizes Bison as a former underground producer and lists gold as its primary commodity, with lead and zinc also noted. Precise sinking date, production totals and present shaft-collar condition remain unverified. Historical references to the Bison Mining Company are not treated as proof that all of its production came from this specific shaft.

sites.name: Blind Tom Mine
overview: On Iron Hill near Leadville, Blind Tom Mine has a history preserved in original mining journals and federal geological records. In 1892 it was reported under lease, with a newly encountered narrow ore vein. Records from 1914 and 1915 show later production, including oxidized zinc ore. Blind Tom also gave its name to a mining company whose holdings included neighboring—but separate—mines. The map pin shows the approximate historic locality rather than a verified mine entrance.

timeline.text: John S. Reid incorporated the Blind Tom Company, which held 20 acres including Blind Tom and the separate Frio and Poor Old Soldier mines; the exact incorporation year is not given.
A contemporary mining journal reported the Blind Tom on Iron Hill under lease to Dr. MacLean for several months and a reported six-inch chloride-bearing vein.
A contemporary report of Iron Silver Mining Company's 1914 results listed 395 tons of Blind Tom ore with reported value of $1,549.
USGS records Blind Tom among Leadville mines producing oxidized zinc ores in both years.
A railway historical compilation lists abandonment of a 2.44-mile three-rail Leadville-to-Blind-Tom-Mine track; this is not evidence that mining ceased that year.

moreHistory: Blind Tom was an Iron Hill property within the Leadville mining district. A historical biography says John S. Reid organized a company whose 20-acre holdings included the Blind Tom, Frio, and Poor Old Soldier mines. In April 1892 a mining trade journal described a lease to Dr. MacLean and reported a narrow chloride-bearing vein. Iron Silver Mining Company's 1914 property breakdown, published in 1915, lists 395 tons of ore and a value of $1,549 for Blind Tom. USGS Bulletin 681 identifies Blind Tom as an oxidized-zinc-ore producer in 1914 and 1915. A later railroad-history compilation lists a 2.44-mile rail connection to the mine as abandoned in 1936, without establishing mine closure. A local tourism account says the mine took its name from a blind mule and identifies a headframe near Graham Park; its 1860 lightning anecdote is chronologically suspect and is not treated as established history. MRDS labels a manganese surface mine while period accounts describe other ore and underground workings; exact relationships among phases and structures remain uncertain.

sites.name: Bohn Mine
overview: Bohn Mine was part of historic underground mining around Leadville. Contemporary accounts place the Bohn name in the 1896 wage dispute, a 1906 mineral-rights court case, and downtown mine production in 1917–1918. Its mapped location is approximate, and nearby Bon Air must be treated separately.
moreHistory: The Bohn was named among Leadville silver-lead mines involved in the 1896 miners wage strike. In 1906 the Colorado Supreme Court ruled against Leadville's claim to ore mined deep beneath its streets in a case involving Bohn Mining Company; direct linkage of that company to the precise mapped mine point remains unverified. The Colorado mine inspector named Bohn shaft among subleased downtown workings producing ore in 1917–1918, without reporting Bohn-specific tonnage. A separate 1899 report says the nearby Bon Air shaft was formerly called Bohn, creating a naming ambiguity that does not justify transferring Bon Air's rescue history here.

sites.name: Bon Air Mine
overview: Beneath Leadville's streets, Bon Air was part of an interconnected network of deep shafts and ore workings. Its most dramatic recorded event came in March 1899, when a cave-in trapped two miners underground for two weeks. Rescuers dug a parallel shaft and reached them alive on March 23. The mine later contributed to the downtown basin's renewed production after difficult dewatering, with period reports describing iron and lead-silver ore and extensive underground exploration. Historic USGS records preserve its geology and relationship to nearby shafts. The map pin marks only the approximate mine locality, not a confirmed entrance or a safe place to enter.

timeline.text: A later state mine-inspector account reported that the shaft had been partly retimbered in 1886; this was cited in an investigation of the 1899 collapse, not as proof of an original opening date.
The Bon Air shaft caved in, trapping pumpman Charles Ruess and helper Albert Frey underground. Rescue crews started a parallel shaft and worked through the connected Star workings.
Ruess and Frey were rescued alive after roughly 14 days underground through a new rescue shaft and short connecting drift. The mine inspector's account was printed in May 1899.

Home Mining Company worked the downtown Leadville basin through Bon Air, Star and Penrose shafts after extensive dewatering; a contemporary account reproduced by USGS reported about 200 tons per day from Bon Air and Star combined, not Bon Air alone.
Engineering and Mining Journal reported that T. S. Schlessinger's Bon Air lease had cleaned out older drifts and levels and was shipping roughly 50 tons of iron ore daily.

A mining-industry report described lead-carbonate ore opened at Bon Air's 540-foot level and reported two high-value carloads; the assay value is a contemporary claim, not independently verified production accounting.
The Bon Air was listed among Leadville-basin operations using diamond drills in a contemporary mining report.

USGS Bulletin 320 described Bon Air's ore stopes near the White porphyry contact, a working level at elevation 9,669 feet, reported ore bodies 10–25 feet thick and averaging about eight ounces of silver per ton, and the neighboring P.O.S. mine to the east.

moreHistory: Bon Air formed part of Leadville's complex underground downtown mining basin. A contemporary Colorado mine-inspector account printed in May 1899 describes a 475-foot Bon Air shaft, formerly called the Bohn shaft, connected to the Star shaft by a drift. On March 9, 1899, a collapse trapped pumpman Charles Ruess and helper Albert Frey; rescuers used a new shaft and underground connections to bring them out alive after roughly fourteen days, on March 23. By 1900 Home Mining Company was using Bon Air with Star and Penrose after major dewatering work; contemporary reports quoted by USGS attributed about 200 tons per day to Bon Air and Star combined. In 1903 reports identified T. S. Schlessinger's lease, iron-ore shipments, lead-carbonate ore at the 540-foot level, and diamond drilling. USGS Bulletin 320 (1907, p. 55) describes ore stopes above the White porphyry contact, ore bodies reportedly 10 to 25 feet thick averaging roughly eight ounces of silver per ton, and the neighboring P.O.S. workings. Historic operational claims are sourced to the period and should not be treated as independently audited production totals. The mapped mine locality does not locate the historic shaft entrance precisely.

sites.name: Breece Iron Mine
overview: On Breece Hill east of Leadville, the Breece Iron Mine stood apart from the district's famous silver and lead producers. Its hematite- and magnetite-rich ore supplied iron useful to the region's smelters, especially as flux. Federal mining history records Breece Iron as the only paying mine on Breece Hill in 1883, while later mineral-resource records connect the old operation with a broader group credited with roughly 300,000 tons of iron production. The surviving mine locality provides a direct scan target for a distinctive chapter of Leadville's industrial mining story.

timeline.text: USGS historical synthesis records the Breece Iron Mine as the only paying mine on Breece Hill that year.
S. F. Emmons documented the Breece Iron Mine in the USGS monograph Geology and Mining Industry of Leadville, including hematite and magnetite.
Iron replacement deposits on Breece Hill were worked for smelter flux; later MRDS compilation associates Old Breece Iron with the Penn Group and reports about 300,000 tons of iron ore production.

moreHistory: Breece Iron was an unusual Leadville operation because its product was iron rather than the district's better-known silver-lead ores. USGS historical synthesis records that in 1883 it was the only paying mine on Breece Hill. The iron deposits of Breece Hill were magnetite/hematite replacement bodies associated with the intrusive complex; later USGS-derived MRDS compilation for the Penn Group, which includes Old Breece Iron, reports about 300,000 tons of iron ore, mostly hematite, shipped for smelter flux or iron smelting. Contemporary geological documentation by S. F. Emmons in 1886 specifically records the Breece Iron locality and its hematite and magnetite mineralization.

sites.name: Brian Boru Mine
overview: On Printer Boy Hill, Brian Boru was one of the Leadville district's leased mining properties in the early 1880s. A mining report in 1883 described several leases, lead-rich ore and a shaft being sunk. Decades later, USGS geologists mapped its own adit, separate from the nearby Altoona entrance, and found portions of the old workings caved. The marker indicates an approximate historic locality, not an accessible mine entrance.

timeline.text: A contemporary Printer Boy Hill report described five Brian Boru leases, three reaching mineralized ground; an upper lease next to Nellie S. had a 31-foot shaft and reported lead-carbonate ore carrying gold.
Brian Boru was listed among Leadville mines being worked wholly or partly by lessees.

USGS Professional Paper 235 described the Brian Boru adit (P-62) as largely caved, with about 300 feet of then-examinable workings and two small mined-out blanket deposits near the portal. This documents conditions at the time of investigation, not present access.

moreHistory: In May 1883, contemporary reporting described five leases on Brian Boru, three in mineral, and an upper lease near Nellie S. with a 31-foot shaft and lead-carbonate ore reportedly carrying gold. In May 1884 the mine remained among Leadville properties worked by lessees. A 1953 USGS study distinguished the Brian Boru adit from the nearby Altoona adit in the Lillian workings: Brian Boru P-62 was then largely caved, with roughly 300 feet of examinable workings in Leadville dolomite and two mined-out small blanket deposits. Ore details for these later-described deposits were unknown; do not attribute Altoona or Nellie S. production to Brian Boru.

sites.name: Brookland Mine
overview: Brookland Mine was one of the historic workings on Carbonate Hill, part of Leadville's silver-and-lead mining district. By the early 1880s it had substantial underground development, including a deep shaft and steam-powered equipment. Later records describe the Brookland shaft and its connection to neighboring Clontarf workings. Historical accounts of production often combine the two mines, so their figures should not be read as Brookland-only output. The mapped point marks an approximate mine locality, not a confirmed shaft entrance or publicly accessible structure.
moreHistory: Brookland Mine on Carbonate Hill had a shaft described as 483 feet deep with steam hoisting and pumping equipment in an 1883 mining directory. An 1882 newspaper index also records pump installation. During the 1880s the Brookland workings were operationally linked with Clontarf under the Adams Mining Company, but contemporary 1886 reporting clearly names a Brookland shaft distinct from Clontarf, a south drift driven toward Clontarf, and an ore body north of Brookland. A USGS historical account records significant output from the combined Clontarf–Brookland operation; combined production must not be assigned solely to Brookland.

sites.name: Buckeye Mine
overview: On the north side of Leadville’s Fryer Hill, the Buckeye Mine has a documented story stretching from early mine financing to a U.S. Supreme Court ruling. In 1880, owners arranged a $10,000 transfer of a one-eighth stake while development continued. Work had stopped by late 1883, and a two-year lease followed in 1885. That lease became the center of Hill v. Sumner, decided in 1889. Buckeye was still listed among small local mining leases in a Colorado report covering 1915–1916. The map point marks an approximate historic mine locality, not a verified entrance.
moreHistory: The Buckeye Lode was already under development by 1880, when David K. Hill and Edward R. and Edward H. Sumner held interests in the north-Fryer-Hill property. Edward R. Sumner agreed to convey his one-eighth interest to Hill for $10,000, with credits for mine-development expenses and contingent payment provisions. The Supreme Court record describes the financing of shaft sinking and machinery, and says Hill continued development until approximately October 1883. In July 1885, Hill and Robert Esser leased the mine to George A. Jenks for two years. The lease required timbering, drainage, maintenance of underground workings, and royalties of 10% or 25% of net smelter returns according to ore value; these are contractual terms, not demonstrated ore shipments. The resulting dispute reached the U.S. Supreme Court, which in Hill v. Sumner (1889) affirmed that leasing the property counted as disposing of it under the 1880 agreement, triggering the unpaid contractual balance. A Colorado State Bureau of Mines report for 1915–1916 later listed Buckeye among smaller Fryer Hill properties operated by lessees. The report does not provide Buckeye-specific tonnage or a confirmed shaft location.

sites.name: Cady Mine
overview: At the Cady Mine near Leadville, a reported high-grade ore strike helped renew prospecting around Fryer Hill in the early 1900s. The Progressive Mining Company worked the property, and contemporary reports described a shaft about 100 feet deep in January 1903. By March, miners were reportedly following the ore through 150 feet of workings and had removed 125 tons. The mapped point marks the historic mine locality, not a confirmed opening.

timeline.text: Colorado's State Bureau of Mines reported a high-grade carbonate-ore discovery at the Cady mine on Fryer Hill under Progressive Mining Company; it attracted renewed local prospecting.
A contemporary mining journal reported the Cady shaft under development to approximately 100 feet and some lead-carbonate ore reportedly valued around $100 per ton.
A subsequent report stated miners followed the new lead ore strike about 150 feet through Cady workings and removed 125 tons during March.

moreHistory: The Cady Mine drew fresh attention in the early 1900s when Progressive Mining Company reported finding high-grade carbonate ore in a part of Fryer Hill that many prospectors had regarded as unpromising. The Colorado State Bureau of Mines described the reported strike in its 1901–1902 account, noting the interest it stimulated. On January 17, 1903, The Engineering and Mining Journal reported that a new Cady shaft was about 100 feet deep and that some lead-carbonate ore was reportedly worth around $100 per ton. On April 4, 1903, the same journal stated that the lead strike had been traced about 150 feet through the Cady workings and that 125 tons of ore had been removed during March. These are contemporary reported observations and figures, not a verified lifetime production total. Later USGS MRDS inventory classifies the Cady as a past-producing underground mine and separately lists zinc as a tertiary commodity. Exact operating start/end dates, complete ownership chain, and present shaft entrance remain unverified.

sites.name: Carboniferous Mine
overview: On Leadville’s Fryer Hill, the Carboniferous Mine formed part of the Chrysolite company’s network of silver-lead workings. In an 1886 federal geological study, Samuel F. Emmons described an ore body followed eastward through the group to the Carboniferous claim, where Carboniferous No. 1 shaft helped open its eastern portion. The same account identifies Carboniferous among the company’s three most productive claims, but does not provide a separate output figure. Today the available map point identifies the historic mine locality, not a confirmed shaft entrance.
moreHistory: Samuel F. Emmons’s 1886 USGS account identifies Carboniferous as one of nine claims of the Chrysolite Mining Company on Fryer Hill. It identifies Carboniferous, Chrysolite, and Vulture as the three claims responsible for most ore removed from the company property; this is a group comparison, not a mine-specific production total. Emmons traced a substantial shared ore body from the Vulture No. 1 and Eaton shafts eastward to the southeast corner of the Carboniferous claim, describing the ore body as roughly 50 feet wide and 12–20 feet thick on average. The eastern part was opened by Chrysolite No. 3 and Carboniferous No. 1 shafts. Emmons described rich early ore in these shared workings as primarily lead carbonate and silver chloride, with some galena. The claim and its named shaft must remain distinct from neighboring Chrysolite and Vulture workings.

sites.name: Carleton Tunnel
overview: Built to give the Colorado Midland a lower, more practical route beneath Hagerman Pass, the Busk-Ivanhoe Tunnel became one of the area’s unusual pieces of infrastructure to live several lives. It replaced the higher Hagerman crossing, later carried automobiles under the Carleton/Carlton name, and ultimately became part of a transmountain water-diversion system. The east portal near Busk Creek is the best defensible Remnant scan target and preserves the location where this railroad, highway, and water history converge.

timeline.text: Busk-Ivanhoe Tunnel developed as a lower-elevation Colorado Midland crossing beneath Hagerman Pass.
USGS historical account records return to the Busk-Ivanhoe route after severe snow shut the higher Hagerman Tunnel.
USGS historical trail map records the Busk-Ivanhoe Tunnel as being called the Carlton Tunnel and used by automobiles.
USGS Water-Supply Paper records transmountain-diversion measurements at the Busk-Ivanhoe tunnel east portal.
Farm Security Administration photographer Marion Post Wolcott documented the road from Carleton Tunnel near Leadville.

moreHistory: The tunnel was developed as the lower-elevation Busk-Ivanhoe crossing beneath Hagerman Pass to improve the Colorado Midland route. USGS historical mapping records that the Busk-Ivanhoe Tunnel lay 575 feet below the Hagerman Tunnel at about 10,953 feet, eliminating substantial climbing as well as 13 snowsheds and 12 bridges/trestles. The tunnel later became known as the Carlton/Carleton Tunnel and carried automobiles after railroad use ended. By the twentieth century it also served as a transmountain diversion from the Fryingpan/Colorado River side toward the Arkansas basin; USGS water records document measurements at its east portal from the 1920s onward. A 1941 Farm Security Administration photograph by Marion Post Wolcott specifically documents the road from Carleton Tunnel near Leadville, providing primary-period evidence for the Carleton spelling and its highway-era landscape.

sites.name: Castle View Mine
overview: On Leadville's Carbonate Hill, Castle View was more than a name on a mining map. Its workings were documented in the 1880s, and its shaft later served the neighboring Big Chief property. By 1911–1912, Colorado mine inspectors counted Castle View among the hill's major ore shippers. Reports trace a changing mix of iron, lead, zinc and manganese-bearing ore, and describe renewed zinc shipments through Castle View shaft in 1917–1918. Some reported tonnage belongs to groups of mines or shared shafts, not Castle View alone. The map marker indicates the historic locality, not an identified safe entrance.

timeline.text: A contemporary mining report described Castle View workings and a proposed drainage connection to the Henriett & Maid system; the connection's completion was not established.

The Castle View shaft served the Big Chief property; a contemporary report estimated about 150 tons of ore per day through the shaft. This was shaft/Big Chief output, not Castle View-claim-only tonnage.
USGS Bulletin 427 published multiple chemical analyses explicitly labeled as Castle View mine ore.
The Colorado state mine inspector named Castle View among three major Carbonate Hill ore shippers; the reported roughly 600 tons per day was a combined figure for all three properties.
A mining journal reported that Castle View lessee Nicholson sublet work to a group planning to mine oxidized-zone iron ore.
A state mine report documented M. A. Nicholson operating Big Chief and Castle View claims via Castle View shaft and shipping zinc ore.

moreHistory: Castle View was an important Carbonate Hill mining locality active by the late 1880s. In 1888 a trade journal described its existing ore workings and a proposed drainage connection to neighboring mines. In 1905 the Castle View shaft handled ore from the Big Chief property, illustrating shared infrastructure rather than necessarily separate Castle View-claim production. USGS published Castle View ore analyses in 1910. Colorado's 1911–1912 state mine inspector named Castle View as one of three major carbonate-zinc shippers on the hill, with other silver-lead and manganese-bearing iron ores; the report's roughly 600 tons per day applies to all three properties combined. A 1914 report described lessee Nicholson subletting oxidized-zone iron mining, and the 1917–1918 state report documented M. A. Nicholson working Big Chief and Castle View claims through Castle View shaft and shipping zinc ore. These accounts establish a multi-decade, site-specific operational history, but no precise modern shaft entrance is verified.

sites.name: Champion Mill
overview: On Halfmoon Creek below Mount Champion stands the remains of a once sophisticated ore-processing plant. Ore descended more than a mile from the Mount Champion Mine by electric aerial tram. By 1913-1914 the mill could process about 100 tons per day, using crushers, grinding mills, amalgamation plates, classifiers and concentration tables to recover gold and silver before concentrates were sent to Leadville smelters. The surviving mill complex provides a distinct physical scan target separate from the mine workings high above it.

timeline.text: Gold discovery associated with Mount Champion is reported in later historical accounts.
Colorado Bureau of Mines documents the Mount Champion Mill operating at about 100 tons capacity, electrically powered and linked to the mine by a 1.25-mile aerial tram.
Colorado Geological Survey documents the Mount Champion tram as more than 6,000 feet long from the mine to the Halfmoon valley mill.
EPA catalogs the location as the Mount Champion Mill Site, CON000802667, and records no further federal action.

moreHistory: The Mount Champion operation linked a high-elevation gold-silver mine to a substantial electrically powered concentrating mill in the Halfmoon Creek valley. Colorado Bureau of Mines reporting for 1913-1914 describes the mill as sixteen miles from Leadville, connected to the mine by a 1.25-mile aerial tram. Hard quartz and iron-sulphide ore carried chiefly gold and silver with lesser copper and lead. High-grade ore went directly to Leadville smelters while mill ore passed through crushing, grinding, amalgamation, classification and concentration equipment. Concentrates were shipped to the Arkansas Valley smelter. The state report gives the electrically powered plant a capacity of about 100 tons. Colorado Geological Survey Bulletin 17 independently records an electrically operated tram more than 6,000 feet long between the Mount Champion mine and mill. The EPA later cataloged the exact location as the Mount Champion Mill Site.

sites.name: Champion Mine
overview: Champion Mine produced gold, silver, copper and lead high on Mount Champion. USGS records more than 27,000 ounces of gold produced during 1912-1940. The mine and its separate mill were connected by mountain infrastructure. This marker identifies the mine locality, not a verified entrance.

timeline.text: USGS recorded production of gold, silver, copper and lead.
No further production recorded in USGS Bulletin 1636.
USGS noted the road between Champion Mine and Champion Mill had recently been graded.

moreHistory: USGS Bulletin 1636 records Champion Mine production during 1912-1940 of 27,032 ounces gold, 12,731 ounces silver, 30,690 pounds copper and 97,839 pounds lead, with no recorded production after 1940. A road connected the mine to the separate Champion Mill and was graded before the 1980s USGS field survey. Secondary accounts describe an aerial tram connecting the mine to the mill.

sites.name: Chippewa Mine
overview: On Breece Hill east of Leadville, Chippewa Mine was one of the district's long-lived underground mining properties. Reports from 1900 describe new shaft development, followed by ore discoveries and leased mining operations. Remarkably, miners were still shipping gold-, silver- and lead-bearing ore from the Chippewa in 1940. Its mapped position is approximate; the original entrance has not been confirmed.
moreHistory: Chippewa Mine was part of the Breece Hill mining landscape east of Leadville. Contemporary trade journals record new shaft development by Chippewa Mining Company around 1900 and an ore discovery reported in the 1900 season. In 1902 the Chippewa Consolidated Mining Company owned Breece Hill ground worked by Chippewa Leasing Company, receiving royalty income while lessees pursued an ore streak. The mine remained active in 1940, when Nick Randall and Eugene Maki reportedly shipped 100–150 tons monthly of gold-, silver- and lead-bearing ore. These are period reports rather than independently audited lifetime production totals.

sites.name: Chrysolite Mine
overview: On Fryer Hill above Leadville, the Chrysolite became one of the district's notable silver-lead mines. In May 1880, contemporary mining reports described high-grade carbonate ore in the Chrysolite workings and shipments around 115 tons a day. The mine remained identifiable under the Chrysolite Silver Mining Company later in the decade and was subsequently documented in federal geological work on Leadville's oxidized ores. Historic imagery preserved in Lake County's collection provides a direct visual record of the mine.

timeline.text: Engineering and Mining Journal, quoting the Leadville Herald, reported important new development in the Chrysolite, high-grade sand-carbonate ore in the north drift from shaft No. 1, and shipments around 115 tons daily.
Leadville city directory listed the New York-based Chrysolite Silver Mining Company, S. F. Parish general manager, with office and mines on Fryer Hill at the head of East Twelfth.
USGS Bulletin 681 documented the Chrysolite Mine in its study of Leadville oxidized zinc ores.

moreHistory: The Chrysolite was one of Fryer Hill's prominent Leadville mines. Contemporary Engineering and Mining Journal reporting in May 1880 described active development from Chrysolite shaft No. 1 and the Roberts shaft, high-grade sand-carbonate ore, and shipments of about 115 tons per day. By 1888 the Chrysolite Silver Mining Company of New York listed S. F. Parish as general manager, with its office and mines on Fryer Hill at the head of East Twelfth Street. USGS work on Leadville's oxidized zinc ores later documented the Chrysolite Mine and its cerussite-bearing mineralization. The Lake County Public Library preserves a historic image specifically identified as the Chrysolite Mine on Fryer Hill.

sites.name: Climax Mine
overview: High on the Continental Divide at Fremont Pass, Climax became one of the world's most consequential molybdenum mines. Its mineral was vital for tough, heat-resistant steel. First worked in the 1910s, the operation grew from underground tunnels beneath Bartlett Mountain into an enormous open pit. It shut down when demand collapsed after World War I, returned to production, supported steelmaking in World War II, and reopened in 2012 after a 17-year hiatus. The active mine is private industrial property: the marker identifies the mapped pit, not a visitor entrance. See it only from public overlooks and obey posted restrictions.

timeline.text: Charles J. Senter found the mineralized outcrop on the western slope of Bartlett Mountain; the material was not yet recognized as molybdenite.
Colorado School of Mines professor Rudolph George identified samples from Bartlett Mountain as molybdenite.
Early molybdenum ore shipments began in 1915; Climax Molybdenum Company was formed in 1918 and sustained production developed during the First World War.
Mining halted after the First World War as demand fell; the 1933 USGS history dates the shutdown from April 1919 to August 1924.
Production resumed with peacetime steel-alloy demand; the 1933 USGS report documented a 2,000-ton-capacity mill, with roughly 1,000–1,200 tons processed daily in 1930.
Climax molybdenum was important to wartime steel production; History Colorado reports annual mine output valued above $13 million during the 1940s.
An open-pit operation was developed alongside the earlier underground workings, according to the USGS MRDS-derived mine record.
The mine ceased production in 1995. Freeport-McMoRan documented restart work in 2010 and shipment of new concentrate on May 10, 2012.

moreHistory: Charles J. Senter encountered mineralized rock on Bartlett Mountain in 1879; its molybdenite identity was recognized in 1895. Initial ore shipments began in 1915, and the Climax Molybdenum Company was formed in 1918. The metal's wartime value was followed by a demand-driven shutdown in 1919–24, then expansion in peacetime alloy markets. USGS investigators documented the deposit's geology, underground workings and large mill in 1933. During World War II the mine's molybdenum strengthened industrial and military steels. Operations later developed open-pit extraction (MRDS records 1973), and the mine was placed on care and maintenance in 1995. After redevelopment, Freeport-McMoRan shipped new concentrate in May 2012. The historical underground levels and modern open pit are related parts of one mine, not interchangeable points.

sites.name: Cloud City Shaft
overview: Beneath Leadville's streets, the Cloud City Shaft helped reveal the complex geology of the downtown mining district. In 1904 its operators shipped iron and manganese ore used in smelting while deepening the shaft in search of additional deposits. The mine encountered a major fault that took its name from the shaft, and underground water complicated further work. A 1905 report describes an attempted drift connection toward neighboring Home Extension workings. The mapped point is approximate: the original shaft opening has not been verified on the ground.
moreHistory: Cloud City Shaft was sunk within Leadville city blocks as the downtown mining district expanded westward. A report for 1904 names the Empire Tunnel Company of Georgetown as operator and describes shipments of iron and high-grade manganese ore for use as smelter flux. That year the company was also sinking the shaft in hopes of reaching the Midas ore shoot; this is a development objective, not evidence that Cloud City produced Midas ore. A September 1905 mining-journal report describes a drift being driven from Cloud City toward a projected underground connection with the separate Home Extension shaft. USGS Bulletin 320 (1907) documents that the shaft passed through about 425 feet of Wash and Lake deposits and some White porphyry before encountering the Cloud City fault. The fault offset, underground water, and difficulties gaining access to the local pumping association hampered deeper work. The USGS also illustrated Cloud City in a geological section alongside the separate Starr and Alice shafts. No surviving entrance is verified.

sites.name: Continental Chief Mine
overview: High above Iowa Gulch, the Continental Chief Mine was once a productive silver-lead-zinc operation. After years of inactivity it reopened in 1905 under Patrick Mulrooney, and contemporary mining reports described shipments of ore and unusually rich silver discoveries. A later U.S. Geological Survey study mapped its adit, branching tunnels and underground stopes. The approximate mapped mine locality is known, but the original entrance has not been independently confirmed and historic workings may be dangerous or inaccessible.
moreHistory: The Continental Chief, above timberline near Dyer Mountain, produced silver-bearing lead-zinc ores in the Iowa Amphitheater. Contemporary 1905 Engineering and Mining Journal dispatches record renewed development after several idle years under lessee Patrick Mulrooney: deeper work planned in August, reopening and reported shipments of about 50 tons daily by September, high-grade silver ore reported in October and December, and continued winter work. A nearby Maguire tunnel about 200 feet south sought the same ore trend but was a separate excavation. USGS geologist C.H. Behre Jr. documented Continental Chief as mine N-99 in Professional Paper 235 (1953), the largest mine in this type of deposit in Iowa Amphitheater; its eastward adit ran roughly 125 feet before branching to north and south drifts, stopes, and main eastern workings in Leadville dolomite below shale. Legacy MRDS sources report approximately $3 million of production value before 1920, and cite Sunshine Mining's 1980 exploration estimates; these are historical reported figures rather than audited production or modern reserves. Federal exploration-assistance archive lists a 1960 lead-zinc docket for Continental Chief Property, but this does not establish renewed mining. USGS research also documented zinc-bearing clay and oxidized zinc minerals. No verified portal coordinate, access rights, or image-reuse rights are established.

sites.name: Coronado Mine
overview: The Coronado Mine was one of the flashpoints of Leadville’s bitter 1896-1897 miners strike. After the mine reopened during the wage dispute, violence erupted there on September 21, 1896, damaging the mine and helping trigger deployment of the Colorado National Guard. Historic photographs preserve the aftermath, while federal historical documentation connects the Coronado directly to the strikebreaking campaign that followed. The mine’s mapped location on the north side of Leadville provides a defensible historic scan anchor, although the anchor should not be interpreted as proof that an open shaft survives today.

timeline.text: Armed violence at the Coronado Mine during the Leadville miners strike damaged/burned the mine surface works and precipitated calls for state troops.
Sixty-five replacement miners from Missouri arrived and were escorted toward the Emmet and Coronado mines by militia, enabling some mine operations to resume.
The Leadville strike ended after roughly nine months; USGS historical documentation records that the miners did not obtain a uniform $3 daily wage.

moreHistory: The Coronado Mine became a central site in the Leadville miners strike of 1896-1897. USGS historical-trail documentation records that replacement miners were escorted to the Coronado and Emmet mines by Colorado militia after the September 1896 violence, helping the mines resume operation and weakening the strike. Contemporary-period photographic holdings at the Carnegie Library for Local History include an 1896 image explicitly cataloged as the Coronado mine after the blow-up. Denver Public Library chronology records that on September 21, 1896 striking miners attacked the Coronado with rifles and bombs, after which the conflict shifted to the Emmett mine and Governor Albert McIntire called out the National Guard. The strike continued into March 1897. The site therefore has unusually strong, site-specific labor and social history beyond a bare mine identification.

sites.name: Crown Point Mine
overview: On Rock Hill above Leadville, Crown Point was more than another mine name on a map. In the 1880s, its underground ore claims were caught in a dispute over who owned valuable mineral veins beneath neighboring placer ground—a case that reached the U.S. Supreme Court in 1888. Years later, water-filled workings presented another challenge. By 1897, a company leasing Crown Point ground had drained the mine, resumed ore shipments, and reported a new sulfide-ore discovery. Today's mapped location marks the historic mine locality, not a verified open shaft; the area is private land.
moreHistory: Crown Point was a lode mine on Rock Hill, east of Leadville. The Crown Point and Pinnacle claims became parties to a major mining-rights dispute involving the Wells and Moyer placer and Iron Silver Mining Company. The U.S. Supreme Court's January 23, 1888 decision in Iron Silver Mining Co. v. Reynolds (124 U.S. 374) documents claims of ore-bearing lodes and competing rights to mineral veins dipping beneath patented placer ground; it reversed the lower court judgment because relevant title evidence was excluded, not a final determination of ownership of all disputed ore. The 1888 Leadville directory lists Crown Point–Pinnacle Mine on Rock Hill under manager W. G. Wood. In May 1895 contemporary mining reporting described plans to drain the Rock Hill ground through the Crown Point shaft. In March 1897, the Engineering and Mining Journal reported that the Nisi Prius Mining Company had leased Crown Point ground on Rock Hill, successfully drained accumulated water, shipped ore, and opened another sulfide-ore face. Crown Point should not be merged with the separate Pinnacle claim or nearby Crown Point No. 3 dump.

sites.name: Delante Shaft
overview: Delante Shaft tells a lesser-known story of Leadville's mining frontier beneath Poverty Flat. Mining partners Robert B. Estey and S. W. Mudd were driving the shaft by 1895, and competing mineral claims later made the area a focus of a documented 1899 dispute. By 1907 federal geologists described two Delante shafts reaching the limestone contact, revealing underground layers that helped map the district even where rich ore remained elusive. The mapped location is approximate; the original shaft openings and any surviving surface features have not been verified.

timeline.text: Searle Placer owners leased mining rights to Robert B. Estey and S. W. Mudd, who advanced the Delante shaft on Poverty Flat.

A contemporary report describes competing Poverty Flat claim locations and a dispute in which the neighboring Jason claim was reportedly surveyed using the Delante shaft; no final judgment is established by this source.
USGS described Delante Nos. 1 and 2 as shafts reaching the limestone contact and supplying geological information; the No. 1 contact lay more than 100 feet below the nearby Villa shaft contact.
A Leadville newspaper obituary retrospectively listed Delante among mining developer Robert B. Estey's enterprises.

moreHistory: Delante was a shaft-development venture on Poverty Flat, west of Fryer Hill and north of Leadville's historic downtown mine workings. An April 1, 1899 Engineering and Mining Journal account reports that owners of the Searle Placer leased mineral rights to Robert B. Estey and S. W. Mudd in 1895, after which they pushed down the Delante shaft. The account places Delante within a contest over overlapping lode and placer locations: rival claimants reportedly located the Jason claim with a survey incorporating Delante, while Searle parties staked competing claims. It does not establish a final legal ruling. USGS geologists Emmons and Irving reported in 1907 that Delante Nos. 1 and 2 were among Poverty Flat shafts sunk to the limestone contact. Although the group had not yet uncovered major ore bodies in the Blue limestone, the shafts supplied useful subsurface evidence; at Delante No. 1 the contact was over 100 feet lower than at nearby Villa, informing the interpretation of underground structure. A November 1914 Leadville obituary independently lists Delante among Estey's mining ventures. MRDS later records the Delante Shaft as an underground past producer with gold, lead and zinc commodities, but gives no production figures or verified collar survey. Delante Nos. 1 and 2, the Villa and Jason workings, and neighboring Coronado/Sixth Street operations must not be conflated.

sites.name: Denver City Mine
overview: On Fryer Hill, the surviving Wright Shaft headframe marks the Denver City Mine, one of Leadville's nineteenth-century underground silver operations. Contemporary reports show miners deepening the property in 1880 after promising silver assays, and by 1888 lessees were shipping roughly 300 tons of silver-bearing iron ore each month. The unusual surviving headframe makes Denver City more than a name on an old mining map: it gives visitors a recognizable surface feature tied directly to the historic workings below.

timeline.text: A pump transferred from the Shamus O'Brien shaft was started at Denver City; contemporary reporting said sinking would resume and iron encountered in the shaft had returned silver assays as high as 44 oz/ton.
Samuel F. Emmons' Geology and Mining Industry of Leadville documented the Leadville district; modern locality records for Denver City cite this work.
The Denver City property was being worked by lessees and shipping about 300 tons per month of argentiferous iron ore averaging about 13 oz silver.
The distinctive Wright Shaft headframe survives as an identifiable Denver City Mine feature on Fryer Hill and provides a practical visual scan target.

moreHistory: Denver City was an underground silver-bearing operation on Fryer Hill during Leadville's early mining era. In October 1880, the Engineering and Mining Journal reported that a pump transferred from the Shamus O'Brien shaft had been started at Denver City so sinking could resume; iron encountered in the shaft had assayed as high as 44 ounces per ton, with a mill run returning 19 ounces. By November 1888, the journal reported that the Denver City Mining Company property was being worked entirely by lessees and shipping about 300 tons per month of argentiferous iron ore. That ore averaged about 35 percent basic excess and 13 ounces of silver, with reported silver content ranging from 11 to 20 ounces. The site remains unusually legible today because the Wright Shaft headframe survives; local mining-heritage interpretation describes the shaft as about 320 feet deep and the headframe as a distinctive Cornwall-influenced form.

sites.name: Derry Dredge
overview: In 1915, a giant electric dredge began working gold-bearing gravel at the Derry Ranch. Its buckets dug 30 feet deep while the machine floated on a pond it created, leaving mounds of tailings. A crew of roughly 25 lived in nearby cabins. After operations shifted to Box Creek, the dredge was dismantled in 1926. The machine is gone, but its historic Corske Creek mining landscape remains documented by the National Park Service. This map marker is approximate and does not establish visitor access.

timeline.text: Derry family patented and developed the ranch.
Saguache Gold Mining Company acquired the ranch and resumed placer work.
New York Engineering Company purchased the property and began shipping dredge machinery.
The 600-ton Derry bucket dredge began mining along Corske Creek.
Worker cabins built for the dredge crew.
Dredge sold and relocated to Box Creek.
Dredge dismantled.
Derry Mining Site Camp listed on National Register.

moreHistory: Samuel Derry developed a ranch on land patented in 1878. After his son died in 1908, Saguache Gold Mining Company resumed placer mining. New York Engineering Company acquired the land in 1913, transported dredge components from Yonkers, and assembled about 600 tons of machinery in 1915. The electric bucket dredge used 13,000-volt power, dug as deep as 30 feet and floated in a moving excavation pond. The National Register nomination reports 3,500 ounces of gold recovered in its first two months. The company built cabins in 1916 for about 25 workers, and the dredge produced all recorded Lake County placer gold from 1916 through 1923. It was sold to Mt. Elbert Gold Dredging Company in 1923, moved to Box Creek and dismantled in 1926. The associated camp still had dredge tailings, ditches, ponds and cabins at the time of its 2000 NRHP listing.
