sites.name: Diamond Mine
overview: At the head of Evans Gulch, the Diamond Mine preserves a visible shaft-and-headframe target tied to more than a century of Leadville mining. Federal field investigators described its double-compartment vertical shaft and surface hoist remains, while historic photographs show the Diamond and neighboring Resurrection as distinct mines. The Diamond later became part of the interconnected Diamond-Resurrection and Yak Tunnel system, linking this individual shaft to the much larger underground story of Leadville mining, drainage and later reclamation.

timeline.text: U.S. Bureau of Mines study identifies 1916 as the beginning of the Diamond Mine operating period.
Diamond operated as a lead-gold-silver-zinc mine according to the federal abandoned-mine-opening study.
MRDS reports about 0.95 million tons of sulfide ore from the consolidated Diamond-Resurrection property; this is combined-property production, not Diamond-shaft-only output.
Colorado DRMS later reported no excavation at the Diamond Resurrection Shaft since about 1986.
Colorado DRMS reports the Diamond Shaft permit was revoked and its bond forfeited in January 2006.

moreHistory: The Diamond Mine was a lead-gold-silver-zinc operation at the head of Evans Gulch. A U.S. Bureau of Mines field study records operation from 1916 to 1960 and describes the surviving double-compartment shaft, hoist structures and waste dump. The mine became physically and operationally linked with the broader Resurrection/Black Cloud system and the Yak Tunnel. MRDS records later Diamond-Resurrection consolidation and reports combined historic production of about 1.3 million tons of oxide ore from 1879-1917 and 0.95 million tons of sulfide ore from 1936-1956; those figures describe the consolidated Diamond-Resurrection property and are not assigned to the Diamond shaft alone. Colorado DRMS records a later Diamond Resurrection Shaft permit, notes the shaft near the end of the Yak Tunnel, no excavation after about 1986, later flooding after Yak Tunnel blockage, and permit revocation/bond forfeiture in January 2006.

sites.name: Dinero Mine Tunnel
overview: West of Leadville, the Dinero Tunnel is both a surviving piece of Sugar Loaf mining infrastructure and a well-documented example of the long environmental afterlife of hard-rock mining. Driven in the late 1800s, the roughly 3,000-foot tunnel reached the Dinero Shaft and served as a drainage and access route to workings higher on the mountain. In 1909 miners were still pushing an upraise toward an older shaft and preparing to develop ore at the tunnel face. A century later, attention shifted from ore to water: drainage from the abandoned tunnel carried elevated metals toward Lake Fork Creek. Reclamation removed nearby waste rock, and in 2009 a bulkhead was installed deep inside the tunnel to reduce discharge. Modern USGS studies continue to use the Dinero site to understand mine-water movement and remediation in the Sugar Loaf district.

timeline.text: Dinero Tunnel driven primarily for silver, extending roughly 3,000 feet to the Dinero Shaft.
Engineering and Mining Journal reported work resumed; an upraise was being pushed to connect with an old shaft before developing ore at the tunnel breast.
Dinero mine-waste piles in the wetland area were removed/reclaimed upslope; USGS monitored discharge immediately below the tunnel.
A bulkhead was installed about 390 meters inside the Dinero Tunnel to reduce mine drainage.
USGS reported post-bulkhead discharge and zinc/manganese load reductions of up to 97 percent at the Dinero portal and downstream monitoring sites.
USGS continued geophysical and water-quality investigations around the Dinero tunnel and wetland.

moreHistory: The Dinero Tunnel was driven in the late nineteenth century primarily for silver and extended about 3,000 feet to the Dinero Shaft. Contemporary Engineering and Mining Journal reporting from February 1909 recorded that work had resumed at the Sugar Loaf property, with an upraise being driven to connect the tunnel with an old shaft before development of a large ore body at the tunnel breast. Later USGS work describes the Dinero as one of the principal Sugar Loaf district tunnels, used both for drainage and access to higher mine workings. After mining, the tunnel became an important source of zinc- and manganese-rich drainage to Lake Fork Creek. Mine waste near the wetland was reclaimed in 2003, and a bulkhead was installed about 390 meters into the tunnel in 2009. USGS monitoring found the bulkhead sharply reduced discharge and zinc and manganese loads at the Dinero portal, while also documenting hydrologic effects on nearby workings, especially the distinct Nelson tunnel.

sites.name: Dolly B Mine
overview: Dolly B Mine has a longer story than its modest name suggests. The mine was shipping ore by the end of the 1890s, when its owners were also pursuing additional workings nearby. Court records from the early 1900s preserve a dispute among the Connolly brothers over financing and control of the Dolly B mining claims. By World War II, state mining officials described Dolly B as a steady source of lead-carbonate ore, with occasional sulfide shipments. It remained on Colorado's operating-mine lists in 1951 and 1952, later worked under lease from Resurrection Mining Company. The map marker identifies the approximate historic mine locality, not a confirmed shaft entrance; nearby mines and workings are separate sites.

timeline.text: A contemporary mining review reported sustained Dolly B ore output; its owners were also developing a separate shaft on the Board of Trade group.
On August 13, the Connolly brothers entered a written agreement governing interests in their Leadville mining properties, including the Dolly B Group.
A federal court case described the financing and disputed management of the four-claim Dolly B Group; it did not identify a precise shaft location.
USGS leveling surveyors documented benchmarks by Dolly B Mine, including a nearby road and water tank, placing the mine in the historic Evansville/Ibex corridor.
Colorado's mine commissioner described Dolly B as a consistent but smaller shipper of lead-carbonate ores, with occasional sulfide ore shipments.
State records listed Dolly B as an operating mine managed by Sam Shimmin for John Roberts & Associates, with gold, silver, lead and zinc products.
The mine remained listed as operating under Roberts & Company, managed by John Roberts and leased from Resurrection Mining Company; products listed were gold, silver and lead.

moreHistory: Dolly B was producing ore by 1899, when a contemporary mining journal described steady output and its owners' separate expansion toward a Board of Trade group shaft. In 1900 the Connolly brothers formalized financial and property interests in the Dolly B Group; a 1905 federal case later detailed their financing disputes. USGS leveling records in 1911 located the mine along a road near a water tank. During 1942–1943 the Colorado mine commissioner described Dolly B as a steady but modest producer of lead-carbonate ore with occasional sulfide shipments. State operating-mine lists document John Roberts & Associates and Sam Shimmin in 1951, then Roberts & Company under John Roberts in 1952, when the property was leased from Resurrection Mining Company. These records establish continuity of a named operation, not uninterrupted production across all intervening years. Exact surviving workings and entrance are not verified.

sites.name: Dome Mine
overview: On the south side of California Gulch, the Dome Mine was part of Leadville's early lead-and-silver mining boom. By 1881 miners were extracting ore from Dome's underground workings and had driven a connection to the neighboring Rock Mine. The connection mattered: Dome's ore had been raised with a whim, while Rock had more efficient hoisting equipment and an ore house. Contemporary accounts describe a plan to move much of Dome's ore out through Rock. Both mines belonged to the Iron Silver Mining Company, but their combined production figures should not be mistaken for Dome's individual output. Today's mapped point identifies the historic mine locality, not a confirmed shaft opening.

timeline.text: Contemporary reporting described active ore production at the Dome, a northward drift connecting to Rock's first level, and a planned shift to hoist Dome ore through Rock's better-equipped incline.
The Iron Silver Mining Company reported about 75 tons/day jointly from the Rock and Dome mines; no separate Dome tonnage was given.
USGS Monograph 12 documented Dome among the California Gulch mine workings, separately from Rock.
USGS Professional Paper 148 provided later geological context for the Dome incline and associated Rock workings.

moreHistory: In April 1881 the Dome and Rock mines, on the south side of California Gulch, were reported as properties of the Iron Silver Mining Company, producing about 70 tons of ore per day jointly. The Dome had its own incline and was producing ore; a northward drift driven from the Dome connected with the first level of the Rock mine. The Dome's hoisting then used a whim, while Rock had a powered hoister and ore house; management intended to raise most Dome ore through Rock to reduce handling costs. In October 1881 the Iron Silver Mining Company's total output was reported near 200 tons/day, including about 75 tons/day jointly from Rock and Dome. These combined figures must not be represented as Dome-only production. USGS historical geology records preserve Dome as a distinct claim and incline among California Gulch workings.

sites.name: Evelyn Mine
overview: On the Carbonate Hill slope near Leadville, the Evelyn Mine was one of the underground workings searching for rich ore below the district's earlier mining levels. Contemporary accounts describe miners reaching sulfide-bearing rock by 1901, driving the shaft to a reported 1,000 feet in 1902, and following a narrow ore streak in 1905. A 1926 U.S. Geological Survey report later documented a substantial ore body where limestone met the Gray porphyry. Its possible connection to nearby mines was a geological hypothesis, not a proven underground link. The map point marks Evelyn's approximate historic locality, not a confirmed mine entrance.

timeline.text: A contemporary Graham Park mining dispatch reported that Evelyn's shaft had reached sulfide-bearing rock; future ore shipments were anticipated, not yet demonstrated by that report.
The Engineering and Mining Journal reported that Evelyn had sunk to approximately 1,000 feet and was drifting toward a projected sulfide ore shoot.
A December report described a narrow ore streak newly encountered in a lower level; it was not sufficient for steady shipments, and operators continued searching for a larger body.
USGS geologist G. F. Loughlin documented a large Evelyn ore body at the second (Gray porphyry) contact; possible continuity with nearby Wolftone and Castle View ore shoots remained unverified.

moreHistory: Evelyn was an underground mine in the Graham Park/Carbonate Hill area of the Leadville district. A 1901 mining dispatch reported its shaft had reached sulfide-bearing ground. By July 1902, a contemporary report said the shaft was about 1,000 feet deep and that drifts were being advanced in search of a sulfide ore shoot. In December 1905, a narrow ore streak was reported in the lower workings, but it was not sufficient for steady shipments; a larger body was still being sought. USGS Bulletin 779 (1926) described a large ore body at the second or Gray porphyry contact and considered a possible, unproven relationship to Wolftone and Castle View ore shoots. A later USGS report recorded 8–9 oz of silver per ton in a sample from silicified Leadville dolomite at Evelyn in Graham Park, but this cannot be generalized to mine-wide production. Dates of first discovery, operators, verified total output, and the exact surviving shaft entrance remain unestablished.

sites.name: Evening Star Mine
overview: On Carbonate Hill, the Evening Star packed an outsized mining story into a remarkably small claim. A geologist who studied the workings firsthand in 1882 described a property of less than five acres that happened to cross the thickest, richest part of the local ore body. Much of its great bonanza had already been removed by then, leaving large timbered underground spaces, but crews were still shipping ore from smaller branches and prospecting for more. The mine used several shafts and sat directly beside the Morning Star, with the Catalpa to the south—neighbors that historical records clearly distinguish from the Evening Star itself. By 1888 the Evening Star Mining Company was still listed on Carbonate Hill under general manager H. S. Dickerman.

timeline.text: Louis D. Ricketts studied the Evening Star underground for several months; by October-November the great main ore body had largely been removed, while ore shipments and prospecting continued.
Ricketts published a detailed study of the Morning and Evening Star mines, documenting Evening Star geometry, shafts, geology, and exceptionally thick rich ore.
The Leadville city directory listed the Evening Star Mining Company, H. S. Dickerman general manager, with its office and mine on Carbonate Hill.

moreHistory: The Evening Star was one of Carbonate Hill's early and unusually rich mines. In 1882-83, geologist Louis D. Ricketts spent months studying the Evening Star and neighboring Morning Star underground. He described Evening Star as less than five acres, about 1,305 feet long by 163 feet wide, yet positioned across the thickest and richest portion of the local ore body. By late 1882 its great bonanza had largely been removed, leaving extensive timbered stopes, while shipments continued from smaller ore branches and prospecting sought additional bodies. Ricketts documented the mine as being worked principally through four shafts, with additional shafts/prospects used for development and geological study. The mine remained an identifiable operating property later in the decade: the 1888 Leadville city directory listed the Evening Star Mining Company under general manager H. S. Dickerman, with its office and mine on Carbonate Hill. Federal geological literature likewise listed Evening Star among the principal Carbonate Hill mines. These records establish a substantial site-specific story without conflating the adjacent Morning Star, Catalpa, or other nearby workings.

sites.name: Fanny Rawlings Mine
overview: Fanny Rawlings is more than a name on an old map: it is a documented Breece Hill mine with surviving industrial remains and a history that spans renewed development in the 1890s through another leasing campaign in 1915. Contemporary mining reports record new machinery, drifting and plans to deepen the shaft in 1895, then identify Fanny Rawlings as one of Breece Hill’s important late-1890s discoveries. A later lease tied its redevelopment to operators of the nearby Big Four. Mining-history field documentation still identifies the mine’s hoist, boiler and headframe ruins and notes that its gold ore once traveled by tramway down toward Evans Gulch.

timeline.text: Engineering and Mining Journal reported new machinery installed, active operations underway, a drift being driven, and plans to deepen the shaft.
Fanny Rawlings was identified as one of the three most important finds in the Breece Hill section during the year.
Contemporary district reporting continued to list Fanny Rawlings among the active Breece Hill mines.
A leasing company composed of members of the Big Five Operating Company, controller of the Big Four property, secured Fanny Rawlings and planned development.
Mining History Association field documentation recorded the hoist, boiler, headframe ruins and ore-tram context at the site.

moreHistory: The Fanny Rawlings was an active Breece Hill mine by the mid-1890s. Engineering and Mining Journal reported in July 1895 that new machinery had been installed, active operations had begun, a drift was being driven, and the shaft was intended to be deepened. Its 1898 work was later described as one of the three most important finds in the Breece Hill section. In 1900 the journal included Fanny Rawlings among the Breece Hill mines active around the major Ibex operations. In February 1915, a leasing company made up of members of the Big Five Operating Company, which controlled the neighboring Big Four property, secured the Fanny Rawlings and planned renewed development. Later mining-history documentation identifies surviving hoist, boiler, headframe ruins, and an ore-car tramway that carried gold ore down toward Evans Gulch.

sites.name: First National Mine
overview: On Printer Boy Hill above Iowa Gulch, First National Mine was one of Leadville's historic underground workings. State and federal records document shipments of lead and zinc sulphide ores around 1915–1916, while later geologists studied minerals from its shaft dump. A mining-history field tour photographed a First National headframe in 2007. The map pin marks an approximate historic locality, not a confirmed safe mine entrance.
moreHistory: First National was a separately named shaft and claim adjoining Julia-Fisk on Printer Boy Hill above Iowa Gulch. The properties later became associated through First National Gold Mining and Leasing Company, but Julia-Fisk's shaft depths, assays and reopening history are not attributed to First National. The USGS reported lead-sulphide ore shipped from First National in 1915. Colorado's mine inspector reported that First National Leasing Company had dewatered its shaft and was producing a small tonnage of zinc-sulphide ore in the 1915–1916 reporting period. USGS Professional Paper 235 (1953) described arsenopyrite and associated sulphide minerals on the First National shaft dump. A Mining History Association 2007 field-tour gallery identified its historic headframe. Exact dates of establishment, closure and current condition remain unknown.

sites.name: Florence Mine
overview: On Printer Boy Hill, the Florence Mine helped turn Leadville's mineral-rich slopes into an industrial mining landscape. Operating by 1878, its workings produced lead-carbonate ore containing silver and gold. In July 1884 alone, a contemporary mining journal reported that Florence shipped 1,138 tons of ore. The property later joined nearby mines in the Lilian Mining Company, while geological surveys singled out Florence for bismuth minerals and native gold. The map pin marks an approximate historic mine locality, not a confirmed shaft entrance.

timeline.text: Federal mining history reports Florence producing lead-carbonate ores containing silver and gold from this year onward.
The Florence and adjacent mines were consolidated under the Lilian Mining Company earlier in the year.
Florence reportedly produced and shipped 1,138 tons of ore during July.
Emmons's USGS monograph documented the Florence mineral locality and ore mineralogy.

moreHistory: The Florence Mine was already producing lead-carbonate ore carrying silver and gold by 1878, according to a federal mining history. The original property comprised the Florence and J. D. Ward claims. A contemporary August 23, 1884 mining-journal report recorded 1,138 tons of Florence ore produced and shipped in July 1884, making it one of Leadville's leading producing mines that month. Earlier in 1884 the Florence was consolidated with adjacent properties under the Lilian Mining Company; company-wide acreage, shareholders and dividend must not be misrepresented as Florence-only figures. Geological literature describes Florence as an unusual locality for bismuth-bearing minerals and native gold within Leadville's predominantly lead-silver ore system.

sites.name: Forsaken Mine
overview: Forsaken Mine was part of the bustling silver-and-lead mining landscape on Carbonate Hill above Leadville. In 1879 miners worked two shafts, linked underground passages and hauled ore using equipment shared with the nearby Buckeye Belle. The property later became part of the larger Morning Star mining enterprise. An 1883 geologist's firsthand study mapped both the Forsaken and Old Forsaken shafts and recorded the ore-bearing rocks underground. Today the mapped point identifies the historic mine area—not a verified shaft entrance—and should be viewed as a historical interpretation rather than directions into mine workings.
moreHistory: A December 1879 report documented active upper and lower Forsaken shafts with new ore houses and interconnected drifts. The lower shaft was hoisted by an engine on neighboring Buckeye Belle, and reported output had been about 15 tons daily earlier in December. In 1880 Forsaken became one of the lodes associated with the Morning Star Consolidated Mining Company, alongside Waterloo, Buckeye Belle and Half-Way House; the $6 million deed was a conveyance of existing interests, not an independently verified mine valuation. In 1882-83 geologist Louis D. Ricketts studied the Forsaken shaft firsthand and distinguished it from Old Forsaken; he documented the shaft's ore-bearing contact at roughly 80 feet and a lower level about 25 feet deeper, with underground connections to nearby workings. By August 1884 a mining report described two men prospecting in Forsaken with little ore then present. Lead-bearing galena and cerussite are documented mineral species. The Forsaken Shaft is separately named in a later federal historic-resource inventory, within multi-component cultural site 5LK1024. These neighboring workings must not be conflated into a single shaft or their histories attributed indiscriminately to Forsaken.

sites.name: Fortune Mine
overview: Fortune Mine on Little Ellen Hill operated across decades of Leadville mining history. Period sources document its leases, underground development, workforce, and eventual closure. Its mapped location is approximate.

timeline.text: Lease and production
Deeper exploration
Operating recovery
Listed as operating
Reported inactive

moreHistory: Contemporary reports identify leasing and production in 1905, new underground exploration in 1917, recovery from a 1942 fire during 1944, and continued state-listed operation in 1951. A federal report records inactivity by 1953.

sites.name: Garbutt Mine
overview: On Breece Hill east of Leadville, the Garbutt Mine was part of the district's gold belt. Archival underground photographs show miners at work there around the turn of the twentieth century, and contemporary reports record ore shipments by 1899. By 1915–16 the Garbutt Leasing Company was operating the Garbutt alongside its extension and portions of neighboring Ibex ground, employing roughly 100 miners across those workings. Garbutt was also known for unusually fine scheelite crystals, a tungsten mineral, and its distinctive fault-hosted ore vein. The map pin identifies the historic mine locality, not a confirmed shaft entrance; the old workings should not be approached or entered.
moreHistory: The Garbutt Mine was an identified gold-producing operation in the Leadville gold belt by the mid-1890s, preserved in underground photographs in the National Mining Hall of Fame and Colorado School of Mines archive. An 1899 Engineering and Mining Journal district report recorded small ore shipments from Garbutt. During 1915–16, the Colorado State Bureau of Mines described the Garbutt Leasing Company, managed by John Cortellini, working the Garbutt, Garbutt Extension and some Ibex ground. The report gives about 100 workers and approximately 150 tons of gold-, silver- and copper-bearing ore daily for this COMBINED leased operation, not solely the Garbutt shaft. It separately lists Garbutt ore shipping via Ibex Switch. The same report singled out Garbutt for crystallized scheelite, a tungsten mineral. A 1985 mineralogical history based on earlier USGS work describes the Garbutt vein in the Garbutt fault between porphyry and Cambrian shale and the South Ibex stockwork at the second level, with quartz crystals, large pyrite cubes, wolframite and scheelite. These details distinguish the Garbutt from nearby mines even though the Garbutt workings were operationally connected with the Ibex property.

sites.name: Garibaldi Tunnel
overview: At the head of California Gulch, the Garibaldi Tunnel reached deep into Ball Mountain to explore mineralized veins and drain the Sunday No. 2 mine workings. Period reports trace its growth from about a quarter mile in 1903 to 1,500 feet in 1905, while later federal geologists mapped a 2,400-foot passage. The tunnel's story spans prospecting, ore and sulfur-bearing rock, underground engineering and eventual environmental cleanup. A 1995 federal assessment found its entrance collapsed, with a waste-rock pile and old equipment nearby. The map marker is approximate; never enter abandoned mine workings.

timeline.text: W. L. Cooper reportedly resumed work under lease from Garibaldi Mining Company; tunnel was about a quarter mile long.
Tunnel had advanced to roughly 1,500 feet; Bray & Davis reported sulfur-rich pyritic material and prospective sales.
G. F. Loughlin studied and mapped the Garibaldi tunnel.
C. H. Behre Jr. conducted a brief follow-up underground study, aided by E. D. Dickerman.
Colorado state mining report listed Robert L. Jones as Garibaldi Tunnel lessee from ASARCO in the Sunday-Ibex area.
Cultural resource inventory documented site 5LK805; drainage diversions were constructed around portal and waste pile.
Engineering assessment recorded collapsed portal, nearby steam engine remains, ~1.6-acre waste-rock pile and mine drainage issues.

moreHistory: Contemporary 1903 reporting says W. L. Cooper resumed work on Garibaldi Tunnel under lease from Garibaldi Mining Company, with roughly a quarter mile already driven through low-grade iron-bearing material. In August 1905, the tunnel was reported 1,500 feet long; lessees Bray & Davis were negotiating sales of sulfur-rich pyritic iron. The USGS later described a 2,400-foot main haulageway trending N.58°E. from the head of California Gulch toward Ball Mountain, exploring the Weston fault and Sunday vein and providing drainage for Sunday No. 2 workings. Geologist G. F. Loughlin studied the tunnel in 1934 and C. H. Behre Jr. revisited it in 1942. A 1952 Colorado state mining report lists Robert L. Jones as lessee from ASARCO for the Garibaldi Tunnel (Sunday-Ibex area), with gold, silver, lead and zinc as listed products; the report's 'Climax' property-location field conflicts with the documented portal geography and should not be used to relocate the site. A 1990 cultural survey recorded the Garibaldi Mine as 5LK805, found not eligible for the National Register by the Colorado SHPO. The EPA's July 1995 evaluation documented a collapsed portal, adjacent steam engine remains, an approximately 1.6-acre waste-rock pile, 1990-91 drainage diversions and ongoing acidic, metal-bearing runoff. These are historic observations, not claims that the machinery remains visible today.

sites.name: Gordon Mine
overview: High on the slopes west of Twin Lakes, the Gordon Mine followed a narrow quartz vein carrying native gold and other minerals. Early miners worked four underground levels, often chasing the richest pockets rather than extracting every section of the vein. When a state geologist examined the property in the 1910s, parts of the old workings had already caved. A gravity tram had been built but never put into service. Historic diagrams and an ore specimen photograph preserve a rare detailed look at this mine. The map marker shows its approximate historic locality, not a confirmed or accessible entrance.
moreHistory: Colorado Geological Survey geologist J. V. Howell documented Gordon (Gordon-Tiger) during 1915–1916 fieldwork, later published in Bulletin 17 (1918), pp. 95–97. The mine had operated intermittently for decades and was said to have yielded substantial gold, but Howell cautioned that reliable figures for ore value and production were unavailable. Four underground levels followed a well-defined quartz vein striking southwest and dipping northwest, with a variable width of three to eight feet. Free gold occurred with pyrite, galena, chalcopyrite, and some sphalerite. Miners had selectively extracted richer pockets rather than systematically removing ore; by the field examination many workings had caved. A gravity tram was installed at Gordon but reportedly never operated. An 1902 federal appellate case documents a dispute over an execution sale of the Gordon and Bengal Tiger lode claims, which were related properties but separately named claims. A 1906 trade-journal report describes a Sunnyside tunnel as a northern extension of Gordon; it is not evidence that this tunnel was itself one of Gordon's four levels. The historic source includes a vertical section of Gordon workings (fig. 24) and an ore specimen image (fig. 25).

sites.name: Greenback Mine
overview: The Greenback Mine stood among the underground operations of Leadville's Graham Park. Its story reaches back to 1878, when miner Patrick Mulrooney reportedly located the claim. By the early 1900s, contemporary accounts described a shaft more than 1,200 feet deep and plans for a large new hoist. The mine later became a source of pyrite as well as silver-, zinc-, and gold-bearing ores under Western Chemical Manufacturing Company. Historic photographs from about 1920 and 1928 preserve views of the mine and its neighbors. Today's map marker identifies the approximate historic complex, not a verified open shaft or safe access route.

timeline.text: Patrick Mulrooney reported locating the Greenback mine in May 1878.
Mulrooney's biographical account reports a period of Greenback operations.
A contemporary account cited by USGS describes a 1,240-foot shaft and plans for a 750-ton-per-day hoisting plant; actual installed capacity unconfirmed.
Mulrooney's biography describes another sustained period of Greenback operations.
State mining report notes pumping through Greenback and Wolftone shafts to help dewater nearby Robert Emmet workings.
Western Chemical Manufacturing Company purchased Greenback in May, according to the 1917–1918 state mining report.
State mining report documents sulphide, pyrite and silver-iron ore production; a January 1919 trade review confirms pyrite operations in 1918.
A local historical photograph identifies Greenback alongside the distinct Mikado and Wolftone mines in northern Graham Park.
Keystone View Company stereograph depicts the Greenback mine buildings.

moreHistory: According to an 1918 biography, Patrick Mulrooney located Greenback in May 1878 and worked it intermittently, notably in 1894–1898 and 1902–1916. A mining account preserved by USGS describes a 1,240-foot shaft and a proposed 750-ton-per-day hoist for 1902; that is a proposed plant rating, not verified actual daily output. The 1915–1916 Colorado mine report mentions pumping through Greenback and Wolftone shafts to help dewater neighboring Robert Emmet workings. Colorado's 1917–1918 mine report says Western Chemical Manufacturing Company bought Greenback in May 1917 and produced substantial sulphide ore carrying silver, zinc, and gold, pyrite for its sulfur, and some silver-iron ore. A January 1919 trade review confirms pyrite mining by Western Chemical during 1918. Local historical photographs identify Greenback beside the separate Mikado and Wolftone workings around 1920, while a 1928 stereograph documents mine buildings. USGS PP235 names Greenback at Graham Park in a mineralogical discussion. Ownership and production totals beyond the cited periods remain unverified.

sites.name: Harrison Reduction Works
overview: At the foot of Leadville’s main street stood one of the facilities that helped launch the city’s silver boom. Edwin Harrison and August Meyer built the Harrison Reduction Works in 1877 to treat the new district’s rich ores, and Harrison Avenue took its identity from the works at its southern end. The plant became a major early Leadville smelter, survived a destructive 1883 fire, added roasting equipment for difficult sulfide ores, and continued operating until the silver crisis of 1893. Its enormous slag pile outlasted the smelter itself and was later reworked and ultimately removed during cleanup of the California Gulch Superfund site. Today the smelter buildings are gone, but the documented footprint marks a foundational industrial site in Leadville’s transformation from mining camp to boomtown.

timeline.text: Harrison Reduction Works constructed as a branch of the St. Louis Smelting and Refining Company; first furnace operating by the fall.
EPA historical record reports unusually high metal-recovery efficiency among Leadville smelters, though with high fuel consumption.
A destructive fire temporarily shut the works; roasting furnaces for sulfide ores were added after reopening.
Federal mineral statistics report 4,020 tons of lead output from Harrison Reduction Works.
A double elevator was installed to increase the height of the roughly three-acre slag pile.
Harrison interests were sold to National Lead Company, also known as the White Lead Trust.
Works closed during the silver panic.
Harrison Recovery Works established to rework the slag pile, then estimated at about one million tons.
Most of the Harrison slag pile was removed to original grade and relocated during California Gulch cleanup.

moreHistory: Constructed in 1877 as a branch of the St. Louis Smelting and Refining Company, the Harrison Reduction Works helped make large-scale treatment of Leadville carbonate ores practical at the opening of the silver boom. Contemporary 1881 reporting called Edwin Harrison’s plant Leadville’s pioneer smelter and described the rapid growth of the district’s treatment industry around it. EPA historical research states that most Harrison ore passed through the A.R. Meyer Sampling Works; Harrison was reported as the only local smelter processing gold ores, and by 1880 it achieved unusually high metal recovery efficiency, though at heavy fuel cost. A destructive 1883 fire temporarily shut the plant; after reopening, roasting furnaces were added for sulfide ores. In 1887 a double elevator was installed to raise the growing three-acre slag pile. Federal mineral statistics recorded 4,020 tons of lead output from Harrison Reduction Works in 1886. The interests were sold in 1890 to National Lead Company/White Lead Trust and the works closed in 1893 during the silver panic. In 1917 Harrison Recovery Works was established to rework the slag, then estimated at about one million tons. The Harrison slag property later entered the California Gulch Superfund cleanup; most of the slag pile was removed to original grade and relocated to the Arkansas Valley pile in 1998–1999, leaving the historic works footprint largely flattened.

sites.name: Hayden Shaft
overview: On Leadville's Fryer Hill, the Hayden Shaft was one of several openings serving the historic May Queen claims. Mining accounts follow its changing role: silver-lead ore in the 1880s and 1890s, iron-bearing shipments in 1903, and a significant 1910 discovery of high-grade oxidized zinc ore. That zinc discovery helped spur renewed interest in minerals previously overlooked in the district. Hayden was still listed as an operating shaft in 1951, when the Leadville Mine Drainage Tunnel also reached its underground water system. Its mapped position is approximate, and nearby mine shafts are separate historic features.

timeline.text: Historic May Queen and Surprise claims map identifies Hayden as a separate shaft alongside neighboring workings.
Contemporary mining press reports a substantial ore chute accessed through Hayden shaft on May Queen territory, with about 50 tons of ore per day reported.
May Queen lessees work the Hayden shaft and ship lead-carbonate ore from a narrow seam.
New lessees resume work through Hayden shaft and ship iron-bearing material.
Burton, White and Thielen discover and ship high-grade oxidized zinc ore through Hayden shaft, an important milestone for Leadville zinc mining.
State records list Cadwell Mining Company operating Hayden Shaft; drainage-tunnel construction also connects to the shaft's underground water system.

moreHistory: Hayden Shaft served the May Queen mine complex from at least 1880, when a claims map named it as one of several shafts. In 1886 a contemporary report described an ore chute opened through Hayden in May Queen territory, reportedly yielding about 50 tons per day of $50 ore and royalties to Great Hopes. By 1892 lessees were working a roughly 25-inch lead-carbonate seam, and 1903 reports describe new lessees shipping iron-bearing material. In 1910 H. E. Burton, H. K. White, and Alfred Thielen found and shipped high-grade oxidized zinc ore at Hayden, a documented turning point in Leadville's zinc industry, described in USGS Bulletin 681 and Professional Paper 138. Colorado's 1951 operating mine list names Cadwell Mining Company at Hayden Shaft; federal tunnel engineering history records drainage and a lateral connection in 1951. Ore figures are contemporary reports, not verified lifetime production.

sites.name: Helena Mine
overview: The Helena Mine, also written Hellena, worked ore-bearing ground in Iowa Gulch east of Leadville. Before 1909, its shallow workings reportedly produced about $100,000 worth of ore, but water became a serious obstacle. Operators returned in 1928 and 1929, only to shut down in 1930 amid expensive pumping and disputes over the property. By then the main shaft had reached 766 feet. A 1953 U.S. Geological Survey report describes the mine's connection to the Helena fault and the complex geology that helped concentrate ore here. The map pin marks the approximate historic mine locality—not a confirmed, accessible shaft entrance. Nearby mines shown on maps are separate workings.
moreHistory: USGS geologist C. H. Behre Jr. devoted a named section of Professional Paper 235 (1953, p. 139 onward) to the Helena/Hellena Mine in lower Iowa Gulch. The report says earlier shallow operations before 1909 reportedly produced ore valued at about $100,000, but water problems curtailed work. Mining resumed in 1928 and 1929; disputes between the operator and landowners, together with increasing pumping costs, caused shutdown in 1930. The Helena shaft, sunk at the surface trace of the Helena fault, was 766 feet deep in 1930. The mine sits in a structurally complicated zone where the Helena and Weston fault branches intersect other major faults. Behre identified it as the only large Iowa Gulch mine accessible during his investigations. The historical production figure is a reported estimate, not an independently audited total; the mine is distinct from neighboring First National/Julia-Fisk, Clear Grit/Ella Beeler and later Black Cloud workings.

sites.name: Hibernia Mine
overview: On Fryer Hill, the Hibernia Mine was part of the intense silver boom that transformed Leadville in 1880. Contemporary reports describe valuable ore, several shafts, active stoping, shipments, and exploration aimed toward neighboring rich ore bodies. Its location beside famous Fryer Hill properties such as the Robert E. Lee and Matchless helps place Hibernia within one of Leadville’s most productive early mining landscapes.

timeline.text: Contemporary reporting said Hibernia, immediately south of the Robert E. Lee, was producing about 10 tons of ore daily; a 22-ton lot was reported at 392 oz silver per ton.
Rocky Mountain News coverage indexed by Denver Public Library records boundary issues, output, shipments, resumed work, production, and employment at Hibernia.
Engineering and Mining Journal reported multiple shafts; the main Hibernia shaft was about 150 feet deep and tapped the principal ore body.
The mine was drifting west seeking continuation of rich ore bodies associated with nearby Big Pittsburg and Matchless ground.

moreHistory: Hibernia emerged as an active Fryer Hill silver-lead producer during the Leadville boom. In April 1880, contemporary mining reporting stated that the Hibernia joined the Robert E. Lee on the south, was producing about ten tons of valuable ore daily, and had a 22-ton settlement reported at 392 ounces of silver per ton. The consolidation then included the Hibernia, Surprise, and May Queen claims. By early 1881 the mine had multiple shafts: the principal Hibernia shaft was reported at 150 feet and tapped the main ore body, with a large stope north of the shaft. In April 1881 crews were driving west in an effort to encounter the rich ore body known from the neighboring Big Pittsburg and Matchless. Denver Public Library indexing of contemporary Rocky Mountain News coverage records boundary disputes, shipments, work resumptions, daily production, and employment during 1880, corroborating sustained site-specific activity.

sites.name: Home Extension Mine
overview: Beneath downtown Leadville, the Home Extension shaft was part of a busy underground mining landscape. Contemporary accounts from 1901 describe manganese ore in the new shaft; by 1905 workers were developing drifts in this area. During the First World War, reports described high-grade manganese production, shipments to Pueblo, and later a temporary shutdown when the market weakened. Government records also preserve the mine's name on historic maps and a 1944 shaft-water measurement. Its mapped location is approximate: the original shaft opening has not been independently verified, and neighboring shafts should not be confused with Home Extension.

timeline.text: Mining press reported new Home Extension shaft development in Leadville's downtown mining area and manganese ore in the shaft; pumping coordination with nearby Penrose workings was proposed.
Mining press reported underground drift work involving the bottoms of the Cloud City and Home Extension shafts, with a substantial iron-manganese ore body described above the workings.
USGS Bulletin 320 documented Home Extension shaft in its Leadville mining-district study (index references pp. 25 and 55).
A May mining-industry report said the Julia operation at Home Extension found high-grade manganese ore and was shipping approximately 50 tons daily to Colorado Fuel and Iron at Pueblo.

Colorado State Bureau of Mines reported Clarence Jarbeau as lessee and Leadville District Mining and Milling Co. as operator, with five workers and roughly 300 tons of manganese-iron ore shipped monthly before a temporary market-related shutdown.
Historic water-level observations at Home Extension shaft recorded groundwater about 23 feet below land surface; later reproduced in a 1979 USGS report.

moreHistory: The Home Extension shaft was developed in Leadville's downtown mining area by the early 1900s. In 1901 contemporary reports described its new shaft and manganese ore, as well as proposed shared pumping costs with the Penrose mine. In 1905 underground drift work was described at the bottoms of the separate Cloud City and Home Extension shafts. A May 1917 report identified the Julia operation at Home Extension and reported a new high-grade manganese shoot and about 50 tons shipped daily to a Pueblo steel concern. Colorado's 1917–1918 mining report separately recorded the Leadville District Mining and Milling Company, with Clarence Jarbeau as lessee, working five miners and shipping around 300 tons of manganese-iron ore monthly before a market-related temporary shutdown. A later USGS report reproduced a 1944 groundwater depth observation at Home Extension shaft. MRDS separately records zinc as a commodity, without supporting a claim that the documented manganese operations produced zinc.

sites.name: Hopemore Mine
overview: On Breece Hill east of Leadville, Hopemore Mine tells a later chapter of the district's underground mining history. Its gold-, silver-, lead- and zinc-bearing workings were linked to a dedicated processing mill, with documented activity in the late 1980s and 1990s. A modern headframe was photographed during a 2007 mining-history field tour, and the mine later hosted tours demonstrating underground equipment and miners' working conditions. Records disagree on the exact start of production, and the map pin marks an approximate historic locality rather than a confirmed shaft entrance. Do not enter old workings or assume the site is open for tours.

timeline.text: A building permit was obtained for the separate Leadville mill intended to process Hopemore ore.
The mill operator reports that Hopemore Mine and the associated mill began sporadic production, continuing for roughly five years; this conflicts with an MRDS first-production field of 1997.
Colorado mining permit M1990-057 'Hopemore Shaft' was issued to Leadville Mining and Milling, covering the Breece Hill mine and separate mill.
Sunshine exploration files cited in MRDS reported estimated proven/probable mineral reserves; these were estimates, not actual production.
MRDS lists Leadville Mining and Milling as owner and 1997 as first-production year, differing from the mill operator's 1989 chronology.
A Mining History Association field tour documented the modern Hopemore headframe behind Ibex Mine dumps on Breece Hill.
According to the mill operator, Robert Calder/Lockland acquired Hopemore Mine around this time.
Hopemore became known for underground heritage tours led by Bob Calder; mine and mill permit arrangements also changed.
A geotagged photograph documented the named Hopemore Mine locality; its camera coordinates do not locate the shaft.

moreHistory: Hopemore was a polymetallic underground mine on Breece Hill. USGS MRDS-derived data records gold, silver, lead, zinc, copper and iron; it describes the Ibex No. 4 fault vein through the mine area and estimated mineral reserves in 1992, not extracted tonnage. The operator of the related but geographically separate Leadville mill says mine/mill production began in 1989 and continued sporadically about five years, with permit M1990-057 issued in 1990. MRDS records first production as 1997, a conflict not resolved here. A Mining History Association 2007 field tour identified the Hopemore headframe behind Ibex dumps. Around 2008 Robert Calder/Lockland acquired the mine; the site subsequently hosted underground heritage tours. Nearby Ibex, Whites Hill Comstock, and a separate same-name Hopemore record must not be conflated.

sites.name: Irene Number 2 Mine
overview: The Irene No. 2 shaft on Breece Hill was built in the 1950s and extended roughly 1,750 feet underground. Operated by ASARCO, it closed amid weak metal prices in 1957 and reopened in 1965. Later connected underground to the Black Cloud Mine, its steel headframe is a reminder of Leadville's twentieth-century mining era.

timeline.text: ASARCO listed for exploration and development.
Irene shaft closed due to low metal prices.
ASARCO and Resurrection reopened Irene workings.
Separate Black Cloud shaft sunk and production began; later connected to Irene.
EPA identified Irene No. 2 as active.

moreHistory: Built in the 1950s, Irene was a roughly 1750-foot shaft in the Resurrection mining complex. The 1952 Colorado report lists ASARCO as operator, John Mitchell as manager, and gold, silver, lead and zinc exploration. EPA records a shutdown in 1957 due to low metal prices and reopening by ASARCO and Resurrection in 1965. The separate Black Cloud shaft was sunk in 1969 and began production in 1971; its workings connected to Irene. A 1986 EPA plan identifies Irene No. 2 as active. Mining historians documented the surviving steel headframe in 2007 and 2017.

sites.name: Jennie June Mine
overview: Above East Tennessee Creek near Tennessee Pass, Jennie June preserves a less familiar chapter of Lake County mining. In 1906, reports described a small crew extracting gold ore and a change of ownership. By 1908, the mine was said to have a 250-foot shaft and underground drifts. A 1934 state report shows renewed interest in the old workings, with equipment being prepared to pump out and repair the shaft. Modern inventories also associate the locality with manganese, though its later mining history remains unclear. The map marker represents the approximate mine area, not a verified shaft entrance; historic mine openings can be dangerous.

timeline.text: Contemporary reporting says a small crew worked through winter and extracted gold ore pending shipment when roads allowed.
The mine was reportedly sold to Pittsburgh investors for $20,000, with a shaft house and machinery planned.
The Jennie June shaft was reported at 100 feet deep in limestone and ore.
A report described a 250-foot shaft, east and west drifts, and gold-bearing ore in the west drift.
Operators planned to resume work after snowmelt at the 250-foot level; resumption was not confirmed.
Colorado's Bureau of Mines reported hoist and compressor installation in preparation for unwatering and repairing the shaft.
The Jennie June Mine name appears on the USGS Leadville North topographic map.
A field guide documented a spur road and photographed the named Jennie June mine locality and cabin.

moreHistory: The Jennie June operation in East Tennessee Park was active by early 1906, when a small crew was reported extracting gold ore. A reported sale to Pittsburgh interests later that year was followed by development of a shaft, which was 100 feet deep by November 1906 and reportedly 250 feet by October 1908, with east and west drifts and gold-bearing ore in the west drift. Operators planned further work at the 250-foot level in 1909. In 1934 the Colorado Bureau of Mines described equipment being installed to unwater and repair the shaft, without confirming production resumed. Later USGS-derived inventory describes Jennie June as a past-producing surface manganese mine; the relationship between that commodity record and earlier gold-bearing underground workings is not fully explained and should not be presented as a single proven production sequence.

sites.name: John Reed Mine
overview: Near Fremont Pass, the abandoned John Reed Mine became known for something smaller than its underground workings: brilliant rose-pink rhodochrosite crystals. Mineralogists were describing its unusually clear red specimens by 1887 and studying their properties in the early twentieth century. A 1961 USGS account recalled crystals as large as half an inch, including a remarkable group of forty from one small cavity. The mine had long been abandoned by then, though occasional specimens could still be found on its dump. Remnant marks the approximate historic mine locality, not a verified safe entrance; the similarly named mine in Park County is a separate mapped feature.
moreHistory: The John Reed Mine in Lake County's old Alicante district is particularly significant in the history of Colorado rhodochrosite. A mineralogical description by G. F. Kunz in 1887, later summarized by Wayland (1942), identified rich-red transparent crystals from this mine. Larsen and Wherry examined John Reed rhodochrosite in 1917, and subsequent mineralogical literature used these specimens in comparisons of crystal properties. USGS Bulletin 846-C (1933) documents the locality in Climax-area geology. Edwin Eckel's USGS 1961 survey called the long-abandoned John Reed mine a well-known source of rose-pink, gem-quality rhodochrosite, describing crystals up to about half an inch and a reported cavity containing forty crystals. Occasional specimens were still found on the dump by that time. MRDS records it as an underground past producer and lists gold, lead, silver, zinc and gemstone commodities, but no verified owners, production totals, or start/end dates have been established. The historic Alicante settlement's tramway and mill must not be attributed to this mine without separate evidence.

sites.name: Josie May Mine
overview: Above Turquoise Lake, the Josie May prospect was a small but geologically unusual turquoise mine. In 1936 it had a 25-foot inclined shaft and scattered prospect pits. By 1951 miners had enlarged the workings and cut a long bulldozer trench. USGS geologists recorded turquoise with green copper minerals and torbernite, a uranium-bearing mineral, in altered rock. Josie May is distinct from the nearby Turquoise Chief mine. The map point shows the approximate historic workings area, not a verified or safe mine entrance.
moreHistory: Josie May was a small turquoise prospect in the St. Kevin/Sugar Loaf area above Turquoise Lake. A USGS account describes a 25-foot inclined shaft and nearby pits at the prospect in 1936. By 1951, the shaft had been deepened, several pits had been enlarged, and a roughly 190-foot bulldozer trench had been excavated. USGS observed water in the inclined shaft and estimated its length from dump material at no more than about 100 feet. The shaft lay at a contact between granite and schist/gneiss. Turquoise occurred along fractures in altered rock. Federal investigators also identified torbernite with turquoise, malachite and chrysocolla at Josie May, while separately documenting metatorbernite at nearby Turquoise Chief. The uranium-bearing occurrence was not regarded as commercially significant. A 2002 geological symposium continued to distinguish the smaller Josie May open-cut workings from the larger Turquoise Chief pit. Regional accounts of 1935 turquoise output should not be treated as verified Josie May-specific production.

sites.name: Julia Fisk Mine
overview: The Julia Fisk is a well-documented Iowa Gulch mine with a surviving surface identity and an unusually clear story spanning early twentieth-century development, deep pumping challenges, lead-zinc-silver-gold mineralization, a 1950s revival, and the 1957 base-metal-price shutdown. Its historic shaft/headframe locality remains distinct from nearby First National and Black Cloud workings.

timeline.text: Principal early mining period; shaft deepened to about 185 m (600 ft).
Silver-bearing galena ore was found around 126 m depth; a deeper gold-bearing fissure was also encountered before pumping costs and organizational difficulties curtailed work.
Colorado mining reporting cited by later locality documentation records the Julia Fisk operating during the year.
Resurrection Mining Co. announced shutdown because of falling metal prices; remaining Julia Fisk cleanup ore was to be mined and milled before underground equipment removal.

moreHistory: Mining at the Julia-Fisk was concentrated chiefly from about 1900 to 1910, when the shaft reached roughly 185 m (about 600 ft). USGS Professional Paper 235 describes a small silver-bearing galena bedding-plane deposit at about 126 m and a deeper gold-bearing fissure, but organizational problems and heavy pumping costs curtailed the early operation. The mine later returned to production in the 1950s. In July 1957 Resurrection Mining Co. told a U.S. Senate committee that falling lead and zinc prices forced an orderly shutdown and that remaining Julia Fisk cleanup ore would be mined and milled before equipment was removed. Later Black Cloud development intersected parts of the Julia-Fisk orebody, but that later mine is not treated as the Julia Fisk scan target.

sites.name: Leadville Mine Drainage Tunnel
overview: Built for wartime mining, the Leadville Mine Drainage Tunnel became something very different: a long-term piece of environmental infrastructure. Federal miners drove the more-than-two-mile drainage adit beneath the northern Leadville district between 1943 and 1952 to lower groundwater and expose lead and zinc reserves. Reclamation took ownership in 1959, and decades later the tunnel became central to treating metal-laden mine water before it reaches the Arkansas River. Blockages and rising mine water triggered a major federal response in 2008, adding another chapter to a site whose story spans wartime mining, water development, pollution control, and river recovery.

timeline.text: U.S. Bureau of Mines began construction to drain northern Leadville mining workings and facilitate strategic metal production.
First construction stage ended after unexpected geologic conditions increased costs and exhausted funds.
Korean War-era extension completed; tunnel reached approximately 11,299 feet.
U.S. Bureau of Reclamation acquired the LMDT for possible use in the Fryingpan-Arkansas water project.
EPA issued an NPDES permit because LMDT effluent contained heavy metals.
Reclamation completed and commissioned the LMDT water treatment plant.
EPA and Reclamation responded to impounded mine water with pumping, a relief well, pipeline conveyance, and treatment.

moreHistory: The U.S. Bureau of Mines began the LMDT during World War II to drain groundwater from the Fryer Hill, Downtown, Graham Park, and Iron Hill portions of the Leadville mining district and improve access to strategic lead-zinc reserves. Work occurred in two stages: the first ended in 1945 after difficult geology exhausted funds, and Korean War demand prompted extension to 11,299 feet by 1952. Reclamation acquired the tunnel in 1959 intending to use its discharge for the Fryingpan-Arkansas Project, but water-rights conflicts prevented that use. Heavy-metal-bearing drainage later required treatment; a treatment plant was completed in 1991 and commissioned in 1992. Partial collapses and blockages created an impounded mine pool, leading to federal emergency pumping and a relief well in 2008. EPA began pumping tunnel water through a 4,700-foot pipeline to the Reclamation treatment plant in June 2008. The LMDT remains a major federal mine-water management feature tied to restoration of the upper Arkansas River.

sites.name: Little Chief Mine
overview: The Little Chief was one of the prominent mines of Leadville's early silver boom on Fryer Hill. Its documented story includes a $300,000 sale bond in 1878, roughly 100 tons of daily ore output reported in early 1880, a dedicated smelter built for its lower-grade ore, and involvement in the dangerous underground mine-fire conditions that affected neighboring Fryer Hill workings. The mine remained identifiable in Leadville records into the late 1880s.

timeline.text: A bond was executed to convey the Little Chief Mine for $300,000, as later recorded in Finnerty v. Fritz.
A smelter was built on Fryer Hill specifically to treat Little Chief low-grade ore; it operated less than a year before unstable ground forced closure.
Engineering and Mining Journal reported Little Chief output at about 100 tons per day and noted a large share went to the Grant Smelting Company.
Engineering and Mining Journal documented the Little Chief manager's ventilation practices during the Fryer Hill underground mine-fire episode.
The Leadville city directory listed the Little Chief Mining Company and placed its mine at the head of East Eleventh on Fryer Hill.

moreHistory: Little Chief emerged during Leadville's first great silver boom. A Colorado Supreme Court case records an October 28, 1878 bond to convey the Little Chief for $300,000, establishing the mine as a valuable, specifically identified property at the beginning of the boom. By March 1880 the Engineering and Mining Journal listed Little Chief at about 100 tons of ore per day and reported that a large portion of its output went to the Grant Smelting Company. The U.S. Mint's 1880 precious-metals report visually grouped Little Chief with the major Fryer Hill mines Little Pittsburg and Chrysolite. The Little Chief also had direct infrastructure: an EPA administrative record, drawing on historical environmental investigation, states that a Little Chief smelter was built on Fryer Hill in 1879 specifically for the mine's low-grade ore, although unstable ground forced it to close within a year after producing an estimated 7,000–10,000 tons of slag. An 1880 Engineering and Mining Journal report further documents the Little Chief manager's controversial ventilation practices during the Fryer Hill mine-fire episode, showing the physical interconnection and hazards of the dense underground workings. By 1888 the Leadville city directory still listed the Little Chief Mining Company, with its office and mine at the head of East Eleventh on Fryer Hill.

sites.name: Little Ellen Mine
overview: The Little Ellen is more than a name on an old map: its 1879 lead-carbonate discovery helped give rise to Stumptown in South Evans Gulch. Contemporary newspaper indexing shows an operating mill by 1881 and rich ore moving in daily shipments in 1882. The mine continued into the twentieth century, and the historic Little Ellen workings remain identifiable within the dense South Evans mining landscape.

timeline.text: Lead-carbonate ore discovery at the Little Ellen; mining-history sources credit the discovery with the beginning of South Evans/Stumptown.
Rocky Mountain News item indexed by Denver Public Library reported the Little Ellen mill operating.
Rocky Mountain News item indexed by Denver Public Library reported rich ore and daily shipments from Little Ellen.
Mining History Association states the Little Ellen operated until 1930.

moreHistory: Little Ellen was discovered in 1879 in South Evans Gulch, a discovery credited by mining-history sources with helping start the settlement later known as Stumptown. By late 1881 its mill was operating, and an 1882 Rocky Mountain News reference indexed by Denver Public Library records rich ore and daily shipments. The mine remained part of the South Evans mining landscape for decades; the Mining History Association states it operated until 1930. Modern local trail documentation still identifies the Little Ellen Incline among the historic mines above South Evans Gulch.

sites.name: Little Jonny Mine
overview: On Breece Hill east of Leadville, the Little Jonny became the core of the Ibex operation and one of the district's best-known gold producers. Earlier silver-lead work gave way to a major gold-producing period in the 1890s. J.J. Brown served as superintendent of the Ibex properties. USGS credits Little Jonny, later the Ibex, with about $13 million in gold production from 1893 to 1923.

timeline.text: Little Jonny claim surveyed.
Actively worked for silver-lead ore carrying gold.
J.J. Brown became superintendent of the Ibex properties.
USGS reports about $13 million in gold production.
Output reportedly reached about $250,000 per month.

moreHistory: Little Jonny began as a silver-lead producer and became a major Leadville gold mine. USGS historical mapping reports about $13 million in gold production from 1893 to 1923 and output up to about $250,000 per month by 1897. Historical mining records document an 1879 survey, Ibex Company development, J.J. Brown as superintendent from 1893, rich gold discoveries, and extensive later workings.

sites.name: Little Vinnie Mine
overview: On Breece Hill, Little Vinnie operated in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. Historical records document an 1879 interest sale, heavy shipments in 1899, leased work in 1902 and later production. The map point is not a confirmed mine opening.

timeline.text: Interest sold
Heavy ore shipper
Leased operations
Recorded production

moreHistory: Contemporary mining journals report sale of five-twelfths interest in 1879 for $10,000, heavy ore shipments in 1899, and work under lease by Vinnie Mining Company in 1902. MRDS reports underground production in 1902 and 1905-06. Entrance, closure date and mine-specific tonnage remain unknown.

sites.name: Little Winnie Shaft
overview: Little Winnie was a historic Leadville underground mine with documented shaft development by 1879. In 1901, a mining journal reported roughly 100 tons of ore hoisted daily, and a mineralized zone extending toward the New Monarch workings. A local heritage guide recalls its lead, zinc, silver and gold production and shipments to a smelter in Salida. EPA records also link its workings to the Yak Tunnel. The mapped point is an approximate mine locality, not a verified shaft entrance.

timeline.text: Shaft and drifts documented in a mining journal.
Contemporary report claims about 100 tons hoisted per day.
Leadville heritage guide describes mine and smelter supply.
EPA records identify Yak Tunnel connection.

moreHistory: An 1879 mining journal described a 46-foot Little Winnie shaft and 70 feet of drifts, with nearby tunnel development. In 1901, another contemporary report stated that Little Winnie hoisted about 100 tons of ore daily and described a sulphide ore shoot extending toward New Monarch. A USGS history includes Little Winnie in the New Monarch group, without assigning all group output to this shaft. A local Leadville historical tour describes gold, silver, lead and zinc production and substantial ore shipments to the Ohio & Colorado smelter at Salida. EPA documents Little Winnie among mine workings connected to the Yak Tunnel system. The mapped shaft location remains approximate; neighboring Winnie, Little Bob, Virginius and New Monarch workings remain distinct.

sites.name: Long and Derry Mine
overview: Long and Derry was part of the early silver-and-lead mining history around Leadville. Miners explored dark, metal-rich rock along Long and Derry Hill, where several closely spaced shafts and tunnels came to be known collectively as the Long and Derry mines. Historical records mention the mines by 1879, document a mining company in 1882, and list the mine among Lake County's silver-and-lead properties in 1915–16. The map marker represents the historic mine locality, not a confirmed entrance. Do not enter abandoned mine workings.
moreHistory: Long and Derry was an early Leadville silver-lead mining locality. A June 1879 contemporary letter mentions the Long and Derry mines, and an 1882 stock certificate documents a Long and Derry Hill Mining Company. The 1886 USGS Emmons monograph and 1953 USGS Behre study describe several closely spaced prospects collectively called the Long and Derry mines: Faint Hope, Diana, Homestake, Gildersleeve, Campbell, Porphyry and Himalaya. The 1953 study describes two shafts about 50 feet deep and a caved tunnel, with galena the main primary ore mineral and cerussite and silver chloride associated with it. A 1912 directory names Hawkins, Long and Derry Mining and Tunnel Company, but exact corporate continuity is unproven. The Colorado Bureau of Mines listed Long and Derry as a silver-and-lead mine with wagon transport to Leadville in 1915–16. Historic accounts concern the named mine group and cannot assign every individual working to one point.

sites.name: Louisville Mine
overview: Louisville Mine on Leadville's Iron Hill was active in the 1880s. Miners developed a lower limestone-hosted ore zone, and J.J. Brown, later husband of Margaret 'Molly' Brown, rose from foreman to superintendent. Historic maps identify this mine locality, but not a safe or confirmed entrance.

timeline.text: Lower ore-zone development documented in limestone; D.H. Moffat and W.M. Clayton identified as Louisville owners.
J.J. Brown superintendent after serving as foreman in 1886.
Directory lists Eben Smith managing Louisville and separate Colorado No. 2.

moreHistory: An April 24, 1886 Engineering and Mining Journal report described lower ore-zone development at Louisville on Iron Hill, following an ore channel in limestone to sulfide ore. The same report named D.H. Moffat and W.M. Clayton as Louisville owners while acquiring the separate Colorado No. 2 mine. The Molly Brown House Museum identifies J.J. Brown as Louisville foreman in 1886 and superintendent by 1887. An 1888 Leadville directory lists Eben Smith as manager of Louisville and Colorado No. 2 mines. USGS MRDS identifies Louisville as a past-producing surface operation with manganese listed. Production totals and an exact mine entrance remain unverified.

sites.name: Lower Printer Boy Mine
overview: On the northwest slope of Printer Boy Hill near Leadville, Lower Printer Boy was part of one of the district's early gold-mining properties. In 1880 a mining journal reported gold-bearing quartz at the lower workings. Later companies tried to revive and combine several neighboring claims; by 1901 plans specifically called for using the Lower Printer Boy shaft. Its history illustrates how early individual claims were repeatedly reorganized into larger mining ventures. The map point shows an approximate historic locality, not a confirmed mine entrance.

timeline.text: A later historical study reports that Printer Boy's northern portion was sold and that Upper and Lower Printer Boy thereafter became distinct names; this is historical context for the split, not proof of a specific shaft date.
Engineering and Mining Journal reported a gold-bearing quartz crevice and gold in washings specifically at the lower Printer Boy.
Lower Printer Boy was named among claims leased or bonded for a new development venture on the north slope of Printer Boy Hill, funded by D. T. Littler.
Printer Boy Gold Mining Company reported plans to use the Lower Printer Boy shaft as part of a group including Upper Printer Boy, Columbia, Miners' Hope and Bradshaw.
A contemporary report described a 20-acre Printer Boy group including Lower Printer Boy and two shafts approximately 500 feet apart; which exact shaft was at the mapped point is not verified.

moreHistory: The Lower Printer Boy was a distinct named portion of the early Printer Boy gold-mining ground. A later historical review describes the separation of Upper and Lower names after a reported sale of the northern portion in 1868. Contemporary reports specifically describe a gold-bearing quartz discovery at the lower workings in 1880, their inclusion in a multi-claim development venture in 1885, and plans in 1901 to work the Lower Printer Boy shaft as part of the Printer Boy Gold Mining Company's grouped claims. The 1901 group reportedly had two shafts about 500 feet apart, but their exact positions are unverified. Claims about exceptional production or giant nuggets from the overall Printer Boy property cannot safely be assigned to this specific lower mine.

sites.name: Lower Waterloo Mine
overview: On Carbonate Hill near Leadville, the Lower Waterloo shaft opened into the Morning Star mine's underground silver-and-lead workings. An 1883 firsthand account describes an unusually well-equipped shaft house, with a Denver-built hoisting engine and pumps to move water from below ground. The mine's ore-bearing rocks included lead carbonate and silver-rich galena, and its workings connected with the nearby Forsaken area. Contemporary mining journals mention Lower Waterloo operations in the 1880s and again among the Morning Star shafts in 1903. The map pin marks an approximate historical locality, not a confirmed shaft opening or public access point.

timeline.text: Lower Waterloo workings were operating as part of the Morning Star property on Carbonate Hill; a contemporary mining journal noted improvement in that portion of the mine.
Louis D. Ricketts examined the Lower Waterloo shaft and workings firsthand, documenting hoisting and pumping machinery and the ore-bearing geology.
The Engineering and Mining Journal reported substantial ore exposure in Lower Waterloo workings and further development of the Waterloo incline.
A trade-journal report still listed Lower Waterloo among the shafts producing on Morning Star territory; its 75-ton daily figure was for the combined shafts, not Lower Waterloo alone.

moreHistory: Lower Waterloo was a distinct shaft and group of underground workings in the Morning Star mining property on Carbonate Hill, not a synonym for the entire Morning Star mine. In a firsthand field study undertaken in 1882 and published in 1883, geologist Louis D. Ricketts identified the Lower Waterloo shaft, described its two-compartment arrangement (one adapted for pumping), and singled out its well-organized shaft house, hoisting engine made by J. W. Jackson of Denver, air compressor, pumps, and ore dumps. His observations connected the Lower Waterloo and Forsaken workings through a common ore-bearing horizon and documented lead carbonate (cerussite), silver-bearing galena and iron/manganese-rich materials. A contemporary January 1883 trade report described substantial ore exposures in the Lower Waterloo workings. In August 1903, a mining report still listed Upper and Lower Waterloo among several active shafts on Morning Star territory, but the reported combined 75 tons per day cannot be assigned to Lower Waterloo alone. The exact original shaft collar is not independently surveyed at the mapped modern locality.

sites.name: Maid of Erin Mine
overview: The Maid of Erin Mine on Carbonate Hill is a well-documented Leadville working whose history spans changing ore economics. Court records tie the named lode to prominent Colorado mining investors in the early 1880s. By 1886, operators were concentrating material from the mine dump that had previously looked worthless, illustrating how improved treatment could change the value of old mine waste. Federal mining history records a large copper discovery on the Maid of Erin and neighboring Henriette properties in 1890, while later geological work documented zinc-bearing minerals at Maid of Erin as Carbonate Hill became important for zinc production.

timeline.text: Colorado Supreme Court case record states H.A.W. Tabor, David H. Moffat, Jacob J.B. Du Bois, James G. Blaine, Jerome B. Chaffee, and Charles E. Rider owned/possessed the Maid of Erin Lode, Survey Lot 568 / Mineral Entry 384.
Engineering and Mining Journal reported a steam concentrating plant at the foot of the Maid of Erin dump producing concentrates from apparently worthless material.
USGS Professional Paper 138 records discovery of a large copper deposit in the Henriette and Maid of Erin properties.
USGS Bulletin 681 documented oxidized zinc mineralization/minerals at the Maid of Erin in its study of Leadville zinc ores.

moreHistory: The Maid of Erin was a significant Carbonate Hill Leadville property with a documented late-19th-century operating history. A Colorado Supreme Court decision records named ownership and possession of the Maid of Erin Lode in 1882-1883 and its formal survey/entry identifiers. An 1886 Engineering and Mining Journal report described a steam concentrating plant at the foot of the Maid of Erin dump producing concentrates from material that had appeared worthless. USGS Professional Paper 138 records discovery of a large copper deposit in the Henriette and Maid of Erin properties in 1890. Later USGS work on Leadville oxidized zinc ores documents Maid of Erin mineralization including smithsonite/sphalerite and related minerals, placing the mine within Carbonate Hill’s later zinc story. These mine-specific records provide meaningful history beyond district context while preserving separation from same-name properties elsewhere in Colorado.

sites.name: Matchless Mine
overview: On Fryer Hill above Leadville, the Matchless Mine links the city's silver boom to the famous rise and fall of Horace and Baby Doe Tabor. Rich ore discovered after Tabor acquired the property turned the mine into a major source of his fortune. As production declined, the Matchless became equally remembered for Baby Doe, who lived for years in the cabin beside the workings. The preserved shaft, headframe, hoist house, powder magazine, and cabin give the site unusually strong physical and documentary context for interpreting Leadville's mining history.

timeline.text: Horace Tabor acquired the Matchless Mine; the National Mining Hall of Fame and Museum dates the purchase to July 17, 1880, and reports discovery of rich ore that September.
The Matchless produced substantial wealth for Tabor; NMHFM estimates about $1.2 million in earnings during this period.
Ore depletion sharply reduced Matchless profits, according to NMHFM.
History Colorado identifies the Matchless Mine with Elizabeth Baby Doe Tabor during this period.
Baby Doe Tabor was photographed at her cabin next to the Matchless Mine and died there that year.

moreHistory: The Matchless became one of the defining mines of Leadville's silver era. The National Mining Hall of Fame and Museum records that Horace Tabor purchased it in 1880 after earlier Fryer Hill successes, that rich ore was found that September, and that the mine generated about $1.2 million for Tabor from 1880 through 1886 before ore depletion sharply reduced profits. History Colorado recognizes the property for both industrial significance as a working silver mine and its social-history association with Tabor from 1879-1899 and Baby Doe Tabor from 1901-1935. Baby Doe later lived at the mine; History Colorado preserves a circa-1935 photograph of her at the cabin beside the Matchless. The surviving shaft/headframe and surface buildings make the historic operation physically legible today.
