sites.name: May Queen Mine
overview: On Fryer Hill above Leadville, the May Queen Mine helped change what miners looked for underground. Its Hayden shaft had already yielded lead ore by 1892. In 1910, a leasing team led by Howard E. Burton found commercially valuable high-grade oxidized zinc ore there. The discovery helped launch a broader search through Leadville's older workings, where zinc minerals once overlooked became important products. Contemporary reports show May Queen was still shipping newly opened zinc-carbonate ore in 1912. The map marker indicates the approximate historic May Queen locality, not an identified open shaft or a public-access route.
moreHistory: An 1880 claims map held by History Colorado documents the May Queen and Surprise claims and names several shafts, including Hayden. In February 1892 lessees at May Queen's Hayden shaft were extracting lead-carbonate ore. In 1910 Howard E. Burton, H. K. White and Alfred Thielen, working a lease at Hayden, discovered high-grade oxidized zinc ore and began shipping it. USGS reports distinguish this breakthrough from earlier, lower-grade zinc finds at the Robert E. Lee mine. By November 1912 contemporary reporting described new zinc-carbonate ore in May Queen's lower level and steady shipments. The mine's history is a documented part of Leadville's shift toward commercial oxidized-zinc production.

sites.name: Midas Mine
overview: Near Leadville's downtown mining district, the Midas Mine was one of several deep underground operations working ore beneath the city. A 1907 U.S. Geological Survey report describes the Midas shaft and the geology of its silver-, gold- and lead-bearing ore. Historical reports describe substantial shipments and later underground work connected to the neighboring Penrose mine. The app marker shows the recorded Midas Mine locality, not a confirmed open shaft or public access point.
moreHistory: The historic Midas mine formed part of Leadville's downtown mining area near the Penrose workings. USGS Bulletin 320 (1907), pp. 48–49, documents a distinct Midas shaft and describes ore in the upper Blue limestone near gray and white porphyry contacts. North of the shaft the oxidized ore zone was described as roughly 20–30 feet thick and 150 feet wide; east of the shaft an ore zone along the Pendery fault reached about 50 feet in thickness, with silver, gold and lead assays. A USGS retrospective describes Midas as a major downtown shipper in its productive period, reporting roughly 5,000 tons a month and mining at approximately 515 feet. A contemporary 25 January 1908 Engineering and Mining Journal account describes a lease of the old Midas property, exploration at the 500-foot level, and ore trammed underground to the separate Penrose shaft for hoisting. The USGS MRDS-derived catalog lists manganese as a commodity and records the mine as an underground past producer, but provides no production dates or mine-mouth survey. Do not confuse Midas with Penrose, Bison, Elk or similarly named mines outside Lake County.

sites.name: Modest Girl Mine
overview: On southern Carbonate Hill near Leadville, the Modest Girl was one of the smaller historic mine workings explored for ore below the hill. Reports from 1884 describe pockets of promising ore. In 1910, miners reported a zinc-bearing zone and plans to follow it from a lower tunnel. A 1926 U.S. Geological Survey study later confirmed that exploration through the Modest Girl shaft had found a small ore body, though no large discovery was documented. The map marker shows an approximate historic locality, not a verified entrance; nearby mines are separate sites.
moreHistory: Period reporting describes limited pockets of good ore at the Modest Girl in 1884. In December 1910 a mining journal reported a five-foot zone of zinc carbonate in upper workings, said to average 40 percent zinc, and a proposal for a lower tunnel; neither grade nor tunnel completion is independently confirmed. USGS geologist G. F. Loughlin later recorded a small ore body found during exploration through the Modest Girl shaft, while noting that the broader southern Carbonate Hill explorations had not discovered large bodies. The historic shaft is distinct from nearby Toledo Avenue, California Gulch, and Thespian workings. USGS MRDS-derived modern commodity metadata lists manganese, while contemporary reporting specifically concerns zinc carbonate; the discrepancy should not be resolved by inventing a production history.

sites.name: Morning Star Mine
overview: On Carbonate Hill, the Morning Star became one of Leadville's notable early silver-lead mines. Period accounts describe it beside the Evening Star and show a substantial underground operation built from a consolidation of claims including Morning Star and Waterloo. By 1880 the company was expanding shafts and underground connections to increase ore output; in 1881 contemporary mining reporting described a $1.3 million transaction involving the property. Its well-documented location, workings, ownership changes, and ore geology make it a strong field-history site while remaining distinct from the neighboring Evening Star and other Carbonate Hill mines.

timeline.text: Contemporary mining reporting described the Morning Star consolidation as a large Leadville mine group and documented active development.
A new east shaft was connected with the No. 5 north drift at about 340 feet, with a station and cages being prepared to increase ore output.
Engineering and Mining Journal reported the Morning Star property sold for $1.3 million and was expected to be consolidated operationally with Evening Star interests.
Samuel F. Emmons documented the Morning Star in the USGS monograph on Leadville geology and mining.

moreHistory: The Morning Star was one of the important early Leadville carbonate mines. A detailed period technical work describes the Morning and Evening Star mines side by side on Carbonate Hill and explains that Morning Star consolidated several smaller claims, especially the old Morning Star and Waterloo. Contemporary Engineering and Mining Journal reporting documents active development and rich carbonate/chloride ore in 1880-1881, including a new east shaft connected to underground workings at about 340 feet and a reported 1881 sale of the Morning Star property for $1.3 million as control shifted toward interests associated with the Evening Star. The mine exploited the Leadville district carbonate replacement ore system and is specifically documented in Samuel F. Emmons' USGS Leadville monograph.

sites.name: Moyer Mine
overview: The Moyer Mine is one of Leadville's historically well-documented Iron Hill workings. Beginning with an 1877 placer location, it became part of the Iron Silver Mining Company's operations and developed extensive underground workings. By the end of the nineteenth century the Moyer was producing iron sulphides and treating zinc-lead ore, linking the mine to Leadville's transition from its early silver boom into the district's important lead-zinc era. The historic property had separate south and north shafts; this record targets the Moyer/south locality and does not merge the North Moyer site.

timeline.text: William Moyer and Judge Wells locate the Moyer placer.
Patent granted for the Moyer placer.
Upper/northern portion sold to Stevens and Leiter as part of Iron Silver Mining Company holdings.
A new ore strike is reported and the lower/south shaft is sunk.
Approximately 2.5 km of drifts had been driven in the Moyer.
Moyer ships zinc to Belgium; Iron Silver Mining Company refits the Moyer concentrating mill for zinc-lead sulphides.
USGS primary leveling records separate South Moyer and North Moyer mine locations.

moreHistory: William Moyer and Judge Wells located the Moyer placer in 1877 and received a patent in 1880. The upper/northern portion was sold in February 1880 to Stevens and Leiter as part of the Iron Silver Mining Company. An 1882 strike was described in the U.S. Mint report; by 1890 about 2.5 km of drifts had been driven. The property included a lower/south shaft sunk in 1882 and a later north shaft about 800 meters away. In 1899 the Iron Silver Mining Company was producing about 200 tons per day of iron sulphides and refitting the Moyer concentrating mill with fourteen Wilfley tables for low-grade zinc-lead sulphides. The Moyer also shipped zinc to Belgium in 1899, an early episode in Leadville's later zinc era. Contemporary and later geological accounts describe substantial sulfide replacement orebodies and pyrite mined as smelter flux.

sites.name: New Monarch Mine
overview: On Little Ellen Hill east of Leadville, the New Monarch grew into an important gold-era mining operation after the 1890s. Its holdings combined multiple claims between South Evans and Big Evans gulches, and period reports describe three working shafts—New Monarch, Cleveland, and Winnie. By 1905 the mine was sending about 200 tons of gold ore per day to an independent smelter at Salida while crews pushed deeper toward sulphide ore. Contemporary reporting later described a large, profitable property with extensive underground development. Mining activity persisted into the mid-twentieth century. Today the surviving New Monarch ore house remains one of the Leadville district's most recognizable mining structures and provides a tangible scan target tied directly to the historic operation.

timeline.text: New Monarch Mining Company reorganization reported; company absorbed Australian and Monarch properties and controlled 32 acres between South Evans and Big Evans gulches.
Contemporary reporting states the operation was working three shafts on Little Ellen Hill: New Monarch, Cleveland, and Winnie.
New Monarch reported shipping about 200 tons per day of gold ore to the independent smelter at Salida; main shaft was being deepened toward sulphide levels.
Engineering and Mining Journal described roughly 100 acres, continuous dividends, and a contract to deepen the Cleveland-area shaft 150 feet from 500 feet.
Colorado state mining report lists New Monarch Lease / Monarch Shaft as an operating gold, silver, lead, and zinc property.

moreHistory: The New Monarch emerged from consolidation during Leadville's post-silver-crash gold era. In 1897 the reorganized New Monarch Mining Company absorbed Australian and Monarch properties and controlled 32 acres between South Evans and Big Evans gulches. By 1904 the operation was working three shafts on Little Ellen Hill: New Monarch, Cleveland, and Winnie. In December 1905 it was shipping about 200 tons per day of gold ore to the independent Salida smelter while its main shaft was being deepened toward lower sulphide levels. A 1907 account described roughly 100 acres on the northwest slope of Little Ellen Hill, credited the company to Timothy Goodwin, Mr. Kortz and associates of the Ohio & Colorado Smelting and Refining Company, described it as a continuous dividend earner, and reported a contract to deepen the Cleveland-area shaft 150 feet from an existing depth of 500 feet. The operation remained active into the twentieth century: Colorado's 1950-51 mining report lists the New Monarch Lease/Monarch Shaft producing gold, silver, lead, and zinc. The surviving ore house gives the site a particularly strong visible connection to this documented history.

sites.name: Niles-Augusta Mine
overview: On Leadville's Carbonate Hill, the Niles and Augusta mines were active in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. In 1888 John H. Simmons was listed as their general manager. By 1901 lessees were shipping about 350 tons of ore monthly from an upper level while exploring deeper ground; another report described work at the 225-foot level and continuing iron-ore shipments. Their workings were geologically linked to nearby Wildcat, although it was a separate mine. The map point marks the approximate historic mining locality rather than a verified mine opening.

timeline.text: Contemporary mining press reported that Niles-Augusta was expected to resume work.
Leadville city directory listed Niles and Augusta mines on Carbonate Hill under general manager John H. Simmons.
Mining press described an ore chute first opened at Niles-Augusta that continued toward adjacent Wildcat ground, complicated by faulting.
Mining journal described Niles-Augusta as actively producing.
Lessees shipped about 350 tons per month from an upper level while searching for the main ore body.
Iron ore shipments continued while a drift at the 225-foot level exposed promising lead ore.
Federal report listed Niles-Augusta among properties affected by broader district dewatering/consolidation activity.

moreHistory: Contemporary sources document Niles-Augusta's operating history on Carbonate Hill. An 1882 mining report anticipated resumed work. The 1888 Leadville city directory names John H. Simmons general manager of the Niles and Augusta mines at the head of East Third Street. An 1894 report describes an ore chute traced from Niles-Augusta toward the adjacent Wildcat ground, where faulting interrupted its continuity; Wildcat remains a distinct mine. The Engineering and Mining Journal called Niles-Augusta an active producer in early 1900. In July 1901 lessees were searching for the main ore body while shipping roughly 350 tons of ore per month from an upper level. In August 1901 reports described continuing iron-ore shipments and exploratory drifting at the 225-foot level where lead ore was encountered. A federal 1915 account lists Niles-Augusta among numerous properties involved in district-scale dewatering or consolidation. The EPA's 1997 cultural-resource assessment identifies Niles-Augusta within a multi-mine historic site grouping, not as a precisely surveyed individual shaft.

sites.name: Oro la Plata Mine
overview: Oro La Plata was a lead-rich silver mine near Leadville's California Gulch, just below the separate Rock mine. By April 1881 it was shipping an estimated 30–40 tons of ore daily. Contemporary reports describe an 800-foot tunnel, a new 70-foot winze, and plans to connect the workings to the Rustin shaft for easier hoisting. Later USGS research documented unusual oxidized zinc mineralization around the mine's older lead stopes. Its mapped point identifies the historic mine locality, not a verified surviving entrance.

timeline.text: Oro La Plata was named among mines supplying ore in the Leadville district.

Contemporary reporting described the La Plata company's mine group near Rock mine, including a tunnel, crosscuts, winzes, and the Rustin shaft; these were company-group workings, not necessarily all on the Oro La Plata claim.
Oro La Plata was reported shipping 30-40 tons of lead-rich ore per day. An 800-foot tunnel, 70-foot winze, and drift toward the Rustin shaft were described.
USGS Monograph 12 documented the Oro la Plata mine in its Leadville district survey.
A USGS study used diagrams of Oro La Plata's oxidized zinc mineralization relative to older lead stopes; this is a study publication date, not a date of mine operation.

moreHistory: Oro La Plata was an active lead-rich silver mining property in the California Gulch/Iron Hill area near Leadville. The Engineering and Mining Journal listed it among producing mines in March 1880. In March 1881 the La Plata Mining and Smelting Company described its nearby three-claim group with a tunnel, levels, winzes and the Rustin shaft; these group workings should not all be assigned solely to the Oro La Plata claim. On April 9, 1881 the journal specifically reported Oro La Plata, situated below the Rock mine, shipping 30 to 40 tons of high-lead ore daily. It described an 800-foot tunnel, a 70-foot winze at its end that exposed sand-carbonate ore, and a drift being driven toward the Rustin shaft to improve hoisting. Emmons's 1886 USGS monograph identifies the named mine, and a 1964 USGS study later illustrated oxidized zinc replacement around lead stopes at Oro La Plata. Neither Rock nor Dome mine production belongs to Oro La Plata; later geological study does not establish continued operations in 1964.

sites.name: Penrose Mine
overview: The Penrose Mine was more than an ore producer: its powerful pumps helped drain Leadville's flooded downtown mines. Begun in 1891, it endured a major labor shutdown and several restarts before an ambitious electrically powered dewatering system went to work in 1915. At its height, Penrose supported a busy network of underground workings and employed about 150 people. Operations faded in the 1920s, and later environmental cleanup altered much of the visible mine complex. This map point marks the approximate historic mine locality, not a confirmed shaft opening or public access point.
moreHistory: Major A. V. Bohn started sinking the Penrose shaft in summer 1891, seeking deep carbonate ore beneath Leadville. The mine helped open the downtown basin before the 1896-97 labor strike halted pumping. The Leadville Pumping Association restarted major drainage work in 1898, enabling nearby mines to reopen. By 1905 the Penrose shaft was reported to be 920 feet deep. The Down Town Mines Company organized in 1914 and installed major electric centrifugal pumping equipment in 1915; the Penrose served as a central drainage point for surrounding mines. Contemporary reports describe substantial lead, manganese, zinc and silver-bearing ores and approximately 150 workers in 1918. Mining weakened amid costs and smelter rates after 1920; major pumps were removed in 1923. Renewed pumping attempts in 1927-29 failed to restore production. Federal cultural-resource investigations in the 1990s documented the Penrose mine-waste dump, shaft foundation, dewatering tunnel and transformer house; cleanup substantially changed the historic surface landscape.

sites.name: Printer Boy Mine
overview: Printer Boy helped revive gold mining around California Gulch in 1868, years before Leadville became famous for its silver and lead. Prospectors found gold in a narrow vein on the slopes above Georgia Gulch, and a stamp mill at Oro crushed ore from the workings. Accounts of rich gold pockets drew investors and miners back to the district, though the most spectacular claims were never fully verified. Over time the property became known as Upper and Lower Printer Boy. This marker identifies the historic mine-group area, not an exact shaft or a safe entrance.
moreHistory: Printer Boy was among the earliest significant hard-rock gold discoveries in the California Gulch district. USGS geologist Samuel F. Emmons recorded the discovery of its gold vein in June 1868 by Charles J. Mullen and Cooper Smith while working for J. Marshall Paul of Philadelphia. The Boston and Philadelphia Gold and Silver Mining Company organized in August 1868, and a stamp mill was erected at Oro to treat its ore. Some later historians suggest that the claim had been located earlier, perhaps around 1861; the date of first staking should therefore remain qualified. Gold occurred in rich pockets in weathered, altered porphyry and quartz with iron minerals; deeper ore included pyrite, chalcopyrite, galena and tennantite. The rich shallow deposits and publicized gold specimens helped renew attention to California Gulch after the early placer boom waned, and contributed to the short-lived resurgence of Oro City. Contemporary reports describe very rich pockets and substantial bullion production, but exact output and some spectacular specimen claims are uncertain and should not be presented as verified totals. The workings were subsequently distinguished as Upper and Lower Printer Boy, and an 1880 observer described the methods as primitive and unsafe. Later Lillian Mines activity in this vicinity is a related historical phase, not evidence that every Lillian ore shipment came from the original Printer Boy workings.

sites.name: Ready Cash Mine
overview: Ready Cash Mine above Iowa Gulch was also known as the Two Mile High adit. It produced gold- and silver-bearing ore, with a reported historic output of $480,000. In 1900 an avalanche swept away buildings near the mine; a blacksmith survived 18 hours buried in snow before rescue. The mapped locality is distinct from the neighboring Big Chicago tunnel.

timeline.text: Houx and Tucker listed at Lake County Ready Cash mine.
Avalanche near mine; blacksmith Sam Kibler rescued after 18 hours.
USGS documents Ready Cash/Two Mile High adit, ore geology and reported output.

moreHistory: Colorado mining directory records Houx and Tucker at Lake County Ready Cash in 1879. USGS PP235 p.148 identifies the Ready Cash or Two Mile High adit, mineralized gold-silver-lead veins in granite and a reported gross output of $480,000 (1934 oral account). Summit County Journal reported an April 1900 avalanche carrying away buildings near the mine and rescue of blacksmith Sam Kibler after 18 hours, reproduced in USDA Forest Service GTR-38.

sites.name: Reindeer Shaft
overview: On the western side of Rock Hill, the Reindeer Shaft helped reopen deep mining ground at Leadville in the early 1900s. The Reindeer Mining Company sank a 500-foot shaft in 1903 to reach ore bodies separated by geological faults. By 1907, contemporary mining reports described roughly 75 tons of daily output. The Reindeer ore shoot also influenced work at nearby mines, including Sequin and Bessie Wilgus. This map marker identifies the approximate historic shaft locality; no surviving shaft opening or public access is verified.

timeline.text: Reindeer Mining Company begins a deep shaft on Wells-Moyer ground, Rock Hill, near but separate from Sequin; 500-foot initial target.
Retrospective reports new Reindeer shaft completed to 500 feet, intended to reach Rock and Dome shoots west of the fault.
Separate Sequin mine reports first shipment from the Reindeer ore shoot, illustrating adjacent interconnected mineralization.
Reindeer listed among prominent Leadville district tonnage producers in year-end review.
Contemporary Rock Hill report estimates Reindeer output near 75 tons daily.
USGS geological study documents Reindeer as part of western Rock Hill mining geology.

moreHistory: The Reindeer Mining Company was sinking a deep shaft on Wells-Moyer ground on Rock Hill by September 1903, reported approximately 400 feet south of the old Sequin shaft and intended initially to reach 500 feet. A January 1904 retrospective reported the new Reindeer shaft completed to 500 feet, aiming to reopen the Rock and Dome ore shoots west of a fault. In December 1905, the separate Sequin mine shipped lead-silver carbonate ore from the Reindeer shoot, illustrating the connected ore geology but not constituting Reindeer Shaft output. A 1906 district retrospective counted Reindeer among the area's major tonnage producers, and a May 1907 Rock Hill report estimated Reindeer output at about 75 tons per day. USGS geological documentation later grouped Reindeer with other western Rock Hill mines. These are historical contemporary reports, not verified cumulative production totals; the present-day condition of the shaft is unknown.

sites.name: Resurrection Mine
overview: The Resurrection Mine was one of the long-lived operations at the eastern end of Leadville’s Evans Gulch. Its story spans the carbonate boom of the 1880s, connection to the Yak Tunnel underground network in the early 1900s, and renewed twentieth-century production under Resurrection Mining Company. The mine worked both oxidized and sulfide replacement ores containing lead, zinc, gold, and silver, and its later history illustrates how Leadville mining evolved from isolated shafts into consolidated, connected underground systems.

timeline.text: The Resurrection operated as an early Leadville manto/replacement mine; later firsthand recollection described it as an old property dating to the 1880s.
The Yak Tunnel workings reached Resurrection No. 1, connecting it to the district underground drainage and haulage network.
Yak Tunnel development reached Resurrection No. 2.
USGS/MRDS reports roughly 0.95 million tons of sulfide ore produced from the combined Diamond-Resurrection operation during this period.
Colorado state records list Resurrection Mining Company, B. B. Greenlee manager, producing gold, silver, lead and zinc at Leadville.

moreHistory: The Resurrection was an old Leadville mine dating to the 1880s, exploiting replacement (manto) and massive-sulfide ore carrying lead, zinc, gold, and silver. The Yak Tunnel reached Resurrection No. 1 in 1908 and Resurrection No. 2 in 1909, integrating the Evans Gulch mines into a long underground haulage and drainage network. USGS/MRDS records report combined Diamond-Resurrection historic production of about 1.3 million tons of oxide ore from 1879-1917 and about 0.95 million tons of sulfide ore from 1936-1956. A 1952 Colorado state mining report lists Resurrection Mining Company, managed by B. B. Greenlee, producing gold, silver, lead, and zinc at Leadville. Metallurgist Frank McQuiston later recalled Newmont acquiring the old Resurrection property during World War II and building an approximately 800-ton mill to treat its difficult lead-zinc-gold-silver ores. Historical photographs preserve the mine buildings and headframe and identify the Resurrection Mine at the head of Evans Gulch.

sites.name: Robert E. Lee Mine
overview: On Fryer Hill above Leadville, the Robert E. Lee became one of the camp's spectacular early silver mines. Contemporary mining journalism in 1881 described a heavily developed property with a shaft exceeding 225 feet, large ore bodies reached by drifts, substantial surface machinery and sampling works, and daily ore shipments measured in dozens of tons. Its owners were reported to have received nearly $1.5 million in dividends after operating and improvement costs. Federal Mint reporting independently records ore shipments from the mine in 1880, anchoring the Robert E. Lee firmly in Leadville's first great production era.

timeline.text: Federal Mint reporting recorded $114,096 in ore shipped from the Robert E. Lee Mine to Golden.
Engineering and Mining Journal later reported output averaging about 90 tons per day during these three months.

Engineering and Mining Journal profiled the mine: roughly thirteen acres, main shaft over 225 feet, recent shipments of 40–50 tons per day, extensive machinery and sampling works, and nearly $1.5 million in reported dividends after expenses.

The Robert E. Lee was listed among leading Leadville mines involved in arrangements for the American Institute of Mining Engineers visit; contemporary reporting also noted federal litigation over a claimed one-third title interest.

moreHistory: By 1880 the Robert E. Lee was already a significant Leadville producer: federal Mint reporting recorded $114,096 in ore shipped to Golden. In May 1881 Engineering and Mining Journal described about thirteen acres on Fryer Hill, a main shaft deeper than 225 feet, 40–50 tons per day of recent shipments, 90 tons per day during September–November 1880, substantial machinery and sampling works, and nearly $1.5 million in dividends after expenses and improvements. The mine remained prominent enough in 1882 to be among the leading mines inviting the American Institute of Mining Engineers during its Leadville visit, while title litigation involving a claimed one-third interest was also reported.

sites.name: Robert Emmet Mine
overview: The Robert Emmet Mine is one of the named historic workings of Leadville's Stray Horse Gulch. Its documented story spans the mature silver-lead era through twentieth-century zinc and later mining activity: it was established by the 1880s, survived the turbulent 1896 Leadville labor conflict, shipped zinc ore under lessees in 1910, changed hands as part of a productive Stray Horse property group in 1916, and was still listed by Colorado under American Smelting & Refining Co. in 1952. A surviving headframe and consistent mine mapping provide a strong physical anchor for interpreting that history on site.

timeline.text: Engineering and Mining Journal listed the Robert Emmet among Leadville mining properties connected with J. B. Wheeler in an ownership dispute.
During the Leadville strike violence, attackers moved into Stray Horse Gulch and attempted to attack the Marian and Robert Emmet mines; the mines were defended.
Robert Emmet leasers temporarily suspended zinc-ore shipments while developing the ore from below for more economical extraction.
Empire Mine Co. purchased a Stray Horse Gulch group including Robert Emmet; contemporary reporting said the included claims had records of large production.
Colorado's state mining report listed Robert Emmet Mine at Leadville under American Smelting & Refining Co.

moreHistory: Robert Emmet was an established Stray Horse Gulch mine by the 1880s. In 1885 the Engineering and Mining Journal listed it among J. B. Wheeler mining properties involved in an ownership dispute. During the violent 1896 Leadville strike, historical accounts place Robert Emmet among the Stray Horse Gulch mines that strikers attempted to attack after the Coronado fighting. By 1910 contemporary reporting described Robert Emmet leasers temporarily suspending zinc-ore shipments so they could attack the ore from below and extract it more economically. In 1916 the Empire Mine Co. purchased a Stray Horse Gulch group including Robert Emmet, Forest City, Result, Gonabroad and Ranchero; the report described those claims as having records of large production and the group as then producing polymetallic ore. The mine remained part of Leadville mining decades later: Colorado's 1952 mining report listed the Robert Emmet Mine under American Smelting & Refining Co. USGS Bulletin 779 also treats Robert Emmet as a named mine in its Leadville ore-deposit framework.

sites.name: Sawatch Tunnel
overview: The Sawatch Tunnel—also recorded as the Siwatch Tunnel—was driven into the Sugar Loaf mining district west of Leadville to explore veins deep beneath the mountainside. By 1912 it extended roughly 4,400 feet and employed 14 miners. Early engineering accounts describe electric mine cars, powered rock drills and timber supports inside the granite tunnel. In 1914 miners reported intersecting the Venture vein and testing gold- and silver-bearing ore, although a later USGS study found only limited production from that tunnel intersection. Its mapped tunnel trace runs northwest from a drainage outlet near Strawberry Gulch. This is a separate working from the nearby Venture shaft and other Sugar Loaf tunnels.

timeline.text: Contemporary mining reporting said the Siwatch tunnel intersected three important veins.
By March, the main tunnel was reported at 4,400 feet, with a west lateral of 700 feet and 14 employees.
In February, reports described an intersection with the Venture vein 580 feet below outcrop and efforts to drain/connect old workings.
An engineering text documented electric-powered drilling and haulage, a roughly 6-by-7.5-foot tunnel in granite, timbered sections, and intermittent development.
In September, a local leasing group reportedly resumed development and found gold- and silver-bearing ore on a raise at the Venture vein.
USGS retrospective documented the Siwatch crosscut and characterized the vein exploration reached by the tunnel as limited in ore yield.

moreHistory: In 1911 the Engineering and Mining Journal reported that three significant veins had been intersected in the Siwatch tunnel. Its March 1912 account described about 4,400 feet of main development, a 700-foot west lateral, and 14 workers. Brunton and Davis's 1914 engineering survey described an approximately 5,000-foot granite tunnel with a 6-by-7.5-foot rectangular section, powered drilling, electric haulage, two-shift work, and roughly 600 feet of timbering; the drive was intermittent and not yet complete. Contemporary reports in February and September 1914 described reaching the Venture vein deep below its outcrop, attempts to connect/drain older workings, and renewed development by local lessees, with reported gold-silver mineralization in a 40-foot raise. The USGS's 1955 retrospective identified Siwatch as a long crosscutting prospect adit that intersected the Gertrude-Venture vein about 400–450 feet below surface; about 400 feet of that vein were explored, with only small quantities of low-grade ore reported at that intersection. These observations do not imply the Siwatch tunnel owned or produced all ore from the separate Venture mine. A 2013 USGS-authored study maps its distinct NW-SE tunnel alignment, and USGS monitored a tunnel-specific drainage site at its southeastern end.

sites.name: Sequin Mine
overview: On Rock Hill east of Leadville, the Sequin Mine was already deep underground by 1882. Historic reports describe a 445-foot shaft and promising lead-silver ore assays. More than two decades later, the mine appeared again in mining news: shipments resumed, and a 1907 discovery brought attention to a new body of carbonate ore containing galena. Contemporary reports distinguish Sequin from the neighboring Bessie Wilgus and Reindeer workings. Its map marker shows the approximate historic mine area, not a confirmed entrance; old workings and nearby land may be hazardous or privately owned.
moreHistory: By February 1882, contemporary reporting described a 445-foot Sequin shaft on Rock Hill and a newly encountered lead-silver carbonate ore body, with assay figures published in the press. The Denver Public Library's historical newspaper index identifies the Leadville and Gunnison Mining Company as an operator in 1882. A December 1905 trade-journal report describes a new shipment of lead-silver carbonate ore associated with the Reindeer ore shoot and Wilgus management; because production is documented in 1882, this should be understood as a later phase rather than the first shipment ever. In July 1906 the mine was among daily ore producers. In January 1907 a new galena-bearing sand-carbonate discovery was reported, with the Sequin described as a regular shipper and located a few hundred feet west of Bessie Wilgus. The USGS MRDS-derived record lists manganese as a commodity, whereas these historical newspaper accounts focus on lead and silver; no unverified explanation is imposed on this difference.

sites.name: Sherman Mine
overview: High in upper Iowa Gulch beneath Mount Sherman, the Sherman Mine represents a much later chapter of the Leadville region than the famous nineteenth-century workings closer to town. A tunnel driven in 1946 was intended to investigate ground beneath the older Hilltop mine system. The resulting Sherman operation became a major silver-lead-zinc producer and remained active into 1982, ultimately credited by the Colorado Geological Survey with roughly 10 million ounces of silver. Its ore formed in an unusual ancient cave system within Leadville Limestone, and the mine became especially famous for striking golden barite crystals. Today the reclaimed mine landscape also tells the story of what happens after mining: waste-rock stabilization and drainage restoration have continued long after production ended.

timeline.text: Leadville Lead Corporation began driving the Sherman tunnel beneath the older Hilltop workings to evaluate deeper mineralization.
The principal modern production period; the mine produced silver, lead and zinc and remained open through 1982.
Sherman Mine closed after a production history credited with about 10 million ounces of silver.
Colorado Division of Reclamation, Mining and Safety completed reclamation to restore Iowa Gulch drainage and stabilize mine waste.
Additional channel-stabilization work was documented to control renewed erosion and protect downstream wetlands.

moreHistory: The modern Sherman operation grew from postwar exploration of the older Hilltop mine system. Leadville Lead Corporation began driving the Sherman tunnel in 1946 beneath the old Hilltop workings to evaluate deeper mineralization. The Sherman Mine later became an important silver-lead-zinc producer; Colorado Geological Survey reports that it remained open as late as 1982 and produced about 10 million ounces of silver over its history. The deposit is notable geologically because sulfide ore occupied an ancient paleokarst cave system in the Leadville Limestone. The mine also became well known among mineral collectors for golden barite and secondary lead-zinc-copper minerals. After closure, the large waste-rock pile and altered drainage in upper Iowa Gulch became a reclamation concern. Colorado reclamation work in 2008 re-established drainage and stabilized waste rock, with later channel-restoration work addressing renewed erosion and sediment movement.

sites.name: Silver Cord Mine
overview: On Iron Hill above Leadville, the Silver Cord was far more than a single hole in the ground. By 1880 its operators reported a deep shaft, thousands of feet of underground passages and regular shipments of silver-lead ore. A later court case gives a rare glimpse of life below ground, describing rail cars on a steep incline, a signaling system and more than a hundred miners. The mine also helped inspire a drainage and haulage tunnel that eventually became part of the much larger Yak system. This map marker identifies the approximate historic Silver Cord mine locality, not a confirmed open entrance.

timeline.text: August mining journal described substantial silver-lead ore in the Silver Cord combination under superintendent Arthur B. Litchfield; reported assays are contemporary estimates.
December report described a 380-foot main shaft, approximately 2,000 feet of drifts, six claims totaling about 60 acres, and regular ore shipments.
Silver Cord Combination Mining Company continued development, with work noted near the Williard claim, Gros shaft and 1,100-foot level.
Colorado Supreme Court decision documented the company's 835-foot rail incline and a workforce exceeding 100 miners; incident occurred before the decision.
Historical reconstruction places completion of the original Blow drainage/haulage tunnel to the Silver Cord incline by June; the later Yak Tunnel was a separate expanded system.

moreHistory: Silver Cord Combination was an extensively developed silver-lead mine on Iron Hill near Leadville. Contemporary mining reports in August and December 1880 describe ore development under Arthur B. Litchfield, a 380-foot main shaft, about 2,000 feet of drifts, six locations totaling roughly 60 acres, a connection with the Cleora shaft, and regular ore shipments. A report from October 1889 describes exploration near the Williard claim, the Gros shaft and the 1,100-foot level. A Colorado Supreme Court decision issued in January 1890 provides an unusual primary account of underground work: more than 100 employees, an approximately 835-foot rail incline, haulage cars and a signaling practice implicated in a worker's injury. The original Blow drainage/haulage tunnel was intended to connect with the Silver Cord incline; a historical reconstruction places this connection by June 1892. Later expansion into the Yak Tunnel system served numerous mines and must not be mistaken for the Silver Cord mine itself. Emmons' USGS studies and mineralogical indexing record silver-bearing galena, cerussite, pyrite and associated minerals at the Silver Cord locality. The site's present-day exact shaft and incline entrances are not established by these records.

sites.name: Smuggler Mine
overview: On the southwest side of Iron Hill near Leadville, the Smuggler Mine worked lead- and silver-bearing ore during Colorado's mining boom. Contemporary accounts described steady production in 1883 and a successful leasing operation the following year. By 1894, miners were sinking a new shaft hundreds of feet through limestone to investigate deeper deposits. A state archive later recorded a map of the mine's underground workings. Its mapped position is approximate; the historic shaft entrance has not been verified, and the area should not be treated as safe or publicly accessible.
moreHistory: In 1883 the Engineering and Mining Journal described Smuggler as a small but regularly producing mine on the southwest side of Iron Hill, enclosed by the Iron Silver, Silver Cord and Iron Hill Consolidated properties, with about $20,000 reportedly in company funds. A May 1884 report identified Mr. Slockett as a successful lessee, with profits estimated in the tens of thousands of dollars. An 1894 report described a newly started shaft about 350 feet deep in limestone, with further sinking planned toward the quartzite contact and a narrow stringer assaying for gold. A U.S. Department of the Interior historical compilation quoted ore grades of 40–60 ounces silver per ton and 35–50 percent lead, figures that should be treated as period descriptions rather than audited averages. The Colorado State Planning Commission's 1936 catalogue lists an undated Smuggler mine workings map associated with a deed to Iron Silver Mining Company, in Sec.30 T9S R79W; the map itself was not reviewed, and no transfer date is established. USGS MRDS lists lead and zinc and categorizes the site as a past underground producer. No specific modern entrance, access right or final closure date is verified. All details refer to the Leadville Smuggler, not Aspen's Smuggler.

sites.name: St. Kevin Mine
overview: The St. Kevin Mine was an important historic silver mine above Turquoise Lake. By 1890, miners had sunk an inclined shaft and followed the ore vein on several underground levels. Later efforts included deepening the shaft in 1914 and driving the nearby Rosse tunnel toward the vein. Historic USGS maps distinguish the St. Kevin shaft from neighboring Grandview shaft and Rosse tunnel. The map pin marks the historically mapped St. Kevin shaft location, not a field-confirmed open entrance; old workings may be unsafe or inaccessible.

timeline.text: Mine map attributed to Jay A. Wilcox showed St. Kevin inclined shaft and workings at 217- and 256-foot levels; separate Grandview shaft accessed a deeper level.
St. Kevin shaft deepened approximately 60 feet to investigate ground below the 256-foot level; results uncertain.
McNair's August survey found the related Rosse tunnel had not yet reached the St. Kevin vein.
USGS reports intermittent output totaling 1,412 tons of ore, based on available records.
USGS Bulletin 1027-E documented the St. Kevin workings, vein geometry, and historic output.

moreHistory: USGS geologist Q. D. Singewald described St. Kevin as among the more productive mines in its district, with historic output possibly approaching one million dollars in value, an estimate rather than an audited total. The mine worked the St. Kevin vein in a Precambrian crystalline-rock setting, with silver the primary objective and some gold. A mine plan attributed to Jay A. Wilcox showed that by 1890 miners had worked from the inclined St. Kevin shaft on levels 217 and 256 feet below the collar. A deeper, separate Grandview shaft reached a level 355 feet below the St. Kevin shaft collar, illustrating the connected vein system but not an identical surface feature. In 1914, miners reportedly deepened the St. Kevin shaft about 60 feet to explore below the 256-foot level; Singewald could not establish the extent or outcome. The related Rosse tunnel was driven to crosscut the vein at a projected depth exceeding 400 feet below the St. Kevin collar, but a survey in August 1917 showed it had not yet reached the vein. Available records listed intermittent production totaling 1,412 tons of ore from 1914 through 1946. These facts concern the St. Kevin mine workings specifically and should not be conflated with district-wide production.

sites.name: Storke Tunnel
overview: The Storke Tunnel was part of the immense underground molybdenum mine at Climax near Fremont Pass. State mining reports named the tunnel in the early 1950s, and by 1961 miners had completed a shaft within the tunnel system to reach deeper levels. It was one part of the workings that helped make Climax a major molybdenum producer. Its mapped portal is distinct from the better-known Storke Shaft headframe nearby. The marker shows an approximate historic portal location, not an entrance to approach or enter.

timeline.text: Colorado Bureau of Mines listed Storke Tunnel as a Lake County molybdenum operation, naming Gibbons & Reed and Boyle Brothers and manager William McGlothlin.
State mining records listed Storke Tunnel as exploration and development work associated with Climax Molybdenum Company.
Mining engineers published a contemporary technical study of the Storke Level's role in Climax's large underground operation.
State report recorded completion of No. 4 Shaft inside Storke Tunnel for 600- and 900-level development and construction of a separate No. 5 Shaft outside the portal.
Mining History Association contributor Mike Kaas later recalled working on the Storke and Phillipson underground levels in summer 1962.
The broader Climax mine shifted from underground block-caving toward open-pit mining; this is context for the Storke system, not a documented exact tunnel closure date.

moreHistory: Colorado Bureau of Mines records separately identify the Storke Tunnel as a molybdenum operation at Climax in 1951 and as exploration/development in 1952, naming Gibbons & Reed and Boyle Brothers and manager William (W. K.) McGlothlin. A 1954 AIME paper details Storke Level operations within the huge Climax underground mine. The 1961 state report records No. 4 Shaft completed within Storke Tunnel to reach the 600 and 900 levels, while No. 5 Shaft was being developed outside the Storke Level portal. A Mining History Association firsthand retrospective recalls work on the Storke Level in 1962. Subsequent mine-wide conversion to open-pit methods changed the context of these workings. The Storke Tunnel/Portal is not identical to the surviving Storke Shaft headframe; mine-wide production totals should not be attributed solely to the tunnel.

sites.name: Sunday No. 2 Mine
overview: High above Leadville on the west side of Ball Mountain, Sunday No. 2 was a historic underground mine with its own shaft, separate from the nearby Sunday No. 1 and Bald Mountain workings. Federal geologists mapped the shafts and surrounding veins, while a 1946 Bureau of Mines survey investigated the district's old mine openings. Decades later, USGS scientists returned to study the abandoned Sunday No. 2 waste pile, documenting ore-related minerals and a barren runoff zone downslope. The map marker indicates the historic mine locality, not a safe entrance or a precisely surveyed opening.

timeline.text: A later mine-history photo caption dates sinking of the Sunday No. 2 shaft to 1904, reporting a cost of $84,000; primary record not yet checked.
USGS Professional Paper 148 maps Sunday No. 2 among the Leadville district workings (Plate 45).

U.S. Bureau of Mines investigated Leadville shafts, including a separately indexed Sunday No. 2 shaft; a modern caption reports lease arrangements and removal of the deteriorated headframe, pending primary verification.
USGS Professional Paper 235 mapped Sunday No. 2 shaft distinctly from Sunday No. 1, along with nearby faults, veins, and tunnels.
USGS surveyed the abandoned Sunday #2 mine-waste pile on Ball Mountain, documenting dump topography and vegetation-damage zones.
USGS characterized Sunday No. 2 mine-waste minerals and later published electrical-property research, keeping Sunday #2 separate from the Venir mine.

moreHistory: The Sunday No. 2 mine occupied the west flank of Ball Mountain above Leadville, at a mapped mine locality around 11,900 feet. USGS mapping (1927 and 1953) distinguishes its shaft from Sunday No. 1 and shows the Sunday vein and adjacent faults/tunnels, but these connected features should not be conflated with a single mine's output. A 2022 historical-photo caption reports the shaft was sunk in 1904 for $84,000 and identifies 1946 Dickerman/ASARCO/Jones-Nylene arrangements and headframe removal; those fine-grained claims are attributed to the caption because the primary 1949 Bureau of Mines shaft subsection was not available for direct review. The 1949 Bureau of Mines RI 4518 is indexed as having investigated Sunday No. 2 in the 1946 field campaign. In 1998 the USGS surveyed the abandoned Sunday #2 waste pile, and in 2000 described a single conical dump in Johnson Gulch Porphyry containing pyrite, galena and sphalerite and a seasonal downslope vegetation-kill zone; in 2003 it published further electrical-property work. This is a distinct and traceable mine site with a documented mining-era shaft and subsequent environmental legacy.

sites.name: Tenderfoot Shaft
overview: Tenderfoot was one of the underground mines east of Leadville. In 1914, a serious cave-in blocked access to its main mining areas. Crews drove a new passage around the damaged ground, and contemporary reports say shipments resumed that October. Historic records also identify manganese mining here, although the exact shaft entrance and total production remain unverified.

timeline.text: Tenderfoot Consolidated Mining Company associated with Tenderfoot, Alps No. 3, and Mary claims in historical compilation; contemporaneous stock certificates corroborate the company's existence but not individual shaft location.
Contemporary mining report states a cave-in interrupted work at Leadville's Tenderfoot mine.
Report describes serious drift cave-in and a new curved bypass drift to regain access to principal stopes; ore described as high-grade lead.
After reopening caved workings, the mine was reported back on the shipping list.
Federal mining review includes Tenderfoot among Leadville-area mines shipping ore.

moreHistory: The Tenderfoot workings east of Leadville formed part of the area's late-19th-century mining activity. A historical locality compilation associates the Tenderfoot, Alps No. 3 and Mary claims with Tenderfoot Consolidated Mining Company in 1880; primary stock records document that company's existence, but the individual claims and shaft collars require separate map verification. USGS-derived mineral inventory lists Tenderfoot Shaft as a past-producing underground manganese mine. Contemporary Engineering and Mining Journal reports provide unusually detailed evidence of a 1914 ground failure: a cave-in interrupted production by June; by August the collapsed drift leading to the main stopes was being bypassed with a curving drift, and the report described high-grade lead ore. By October the mine was reportedly shipping again after reopening the affected ground. A federal review of 1915 mining names Tenderfoot among Leadville mines shipping ore. These sources do not establish an exact shaft depth, verified tonnage, or a surveyed portal position; manganese and lead descriptions reflect different records and should not be collapsed into a single ore-grade claim.

sites.name: Thespian Mine
overview: On the slopes of Carbonate Hill near Leadville, the Thespian Mine illustrates the persistence—and uncertainty—of Colorado's silver-era underground exploration. Mining crews had driven a shaft hundreds of feet deep by 1883. Later reports described silver-bearing iron ore, miles of underground development measured in thousands of feet, and water problems that made extraction difficult. Contemporary journals and a later USGS study tell a nuanced story of small ore discoveries and ambitious exploration rather than a proven bonanza. Its mapped location is approximate; the original shaft entrance has not been verified.

timeline.text: Contemporary mining news reported shaft sinking underway at the Thespian property on Carbonate Hill.
Thespian shaft was reported 590 feet deep; drilling had crossed contact material and entered limestone, with drifting planned.
A trade journal reported low-grade silver-bearing iron ore at about 520 feet, with a winze showing at least 14 feet of ore.
A later USGS account dates a small Thespian ore-body discovery to 1894; chronology is not fully reconciled with the 1891 report.
The old shaft was described as roughly 600 feet deep with over 5,000 feet of drifting; water hampered work and diamond drilling was planned.

moreHistory: Thespian was a deeply developed underground prospect on Carbonate Hill. Contemporary mining reporting records shaft sinking in 1882, a 590-foot shaft by February 1883 and plans to drift along the geological contact. In April 1891 the Engineering and Mining Journal reported a low-grade argentiferous iron-ore body at about 520 feet and a winze showing 14 feet of ore. USGS Bulletin 779 retrospectively identifies a small Thespian ore-body discovery in 1894 and describes limited mineralization overall; the difference in reported discovery dates should not be smoothed over. By June 1900, the old shaft was said to be roughly 600 feet deep, with more than 5,000 feet of drifts between the 565- and 600-foot levels. Some ore had been shipped, but water problems hindered development; diamond drilling was proposed to test lower contacts. Do not conflate these facts with nearby mines.

sites.name: Tucson Mine
overview: On Iron Hill east of Leadville, the Tucson Mine connects the district's early silver boom with its later zinc era. Added to the Iron Silver Mining Company in 1881, the mine developed a shaft about 1,100 feet deep and later yielded exceptionally rich silver ore in its lower workings. Mining shifted toward lead and zinc sulfides in the 1910s, and the property was reopened again in 1940 to recover zinc carbonate left by earlier operators. The surviving mine locality and dump remain identifiable enough that the U.S. Geological Survey used the Tucson dump for a dedicated geoelectrical field study in 2000.

timeline.text: Tucson and Luella properties were added to the Iron Silver Mining Company holdings of W. H. Stevens and Levi Z. Leiter.
The Tucson property was patented by Charles J. Doud and associates.
High-grade silver was mined in lower levels; one reported assay reached 2,000 ounces of silver per ton.
Considerable mining continued, with lead and zinc sulfides becoming principal ores.
Axel Lind and associates reopened the upper shaft to work a remaining zinc-carbonate orebody.
Low-grade lead-carbonate shipments ended and the mine closed again.
USGS published a geoelectrical laboratory and field study of materials from the Tucson Mine dump.

moreHistory: The Tucson became part of W. H. Stevens and Levi Z. Leiter's Iron Silver Mining Company holdings in 1881 and was patented in 1886. Its shaft was ultimately sunk to about 1,100 feet. High-grade silver was encountered in lower workings in 1910, including a reported assay as high as 2,000 ounces per ton, and substantial work continued from 1912 to 1918 with lead-zinc sulfides becoming important. Reopening attempts followed, and in 1940 Axel Lind and associates reopened the upper shaft to recover a remaining smithsonite body; shipments ended after buyer grade requirements increased, while low-grade lead carbonate continued to be shipped until closure in 1944. The mine is also geologically notable for well-documented lead-silver and zinc mineralization and later became the subject of a 2000 USGS geoelectrical study of its mine dump.

sites.name: Turquoise Chief Mine
overview: Above Turquoise Lake, the Turquoise Chief Mine was worked for blue-green turquoise rather than the silver and lead for which Leadville is famous. A historical account says two Navajo miners recovered about 1,000 pounds of turquoise here in the mid-1930s, though that quantity is not independently verified. Later geologists described a sizable open pit and documented the uranium-bearing mineral metatorbernite in the granite. The nearby Josie May workings are a separate mine. This map marker indicates an approximate historical mine locality, not a confirmed entrance or public-access destination.

timeline.text: Reported initial turquoise extraction by two Navajo miners, with approximately 1,000 pounds recovered over two years (Pearl 1951, cited by Modreski & Murphy 2002; reported figure).
USGS report identified metatorbernite disseminated in granite at Turquoise Chief, separate from Josie May mineral occurrences.
Geologists Modreski and Murphy described the Turquoise Chief workings as a relatively large open pit and distinguished Josie May's smaller cuts southwest of it.

moreHistory: Turquoise Chief was worked for turquoise in altered St. Kevin Granite north of Turquoise Lake. Modreski and Murphy (2002), citing Richard Pearl (1951), reported that two Navajo miners first worked the site in 1935 and reportedly recovered about 1,000 pounds of turquoise over two years; this figure is historical reporting, not independently verified production data. The geologists stated excavation apparently continued over roughly the following half century, and described a comparatively large open pit at Turquoise Chief, distinct from the Josie May open cuts to the southwest. In 1953, USGS geologists Pierson and Singewald documented metatorbernite disseminated in granite at Turquoise Chief, distinguishing it from torbernite at Josie May. The turquoise forms veinlets and nodules in weathered Precambrian St. Kevin Granite. Published histories remain incomplete; no current access or operation status is inferred.

sites.name: Venir Mine
overview: On Breece Hill east of Leadville, the Venir Mine—also known historically as South Ibex—followed gold-bearing quartz and pyrite veins deep into the mountain. By 1935, miners had developed four underground levels and extensive drifts. Contemporary reports describe a 75-ton mill at Venir in 1940 and a subsequent plan for larger milling operations in California Gulch. Today the abandoned mine-waste pile preserves a visible trace of the work, and USGS scientists have studied its minerals and environmental effects. The map pin marks the approximate historic mine locality, not a safe entrance. The area includes fragile structures and potentially hazardous openings; respect property boundaries and stay out of mine workings.

timeline.text: Venir/South Ibex operated intermittently; underground development reached four levels with intervening stopes.
John Cortellini supplied reported assays for low-grade mineralized rock near the Venir shaft; these were estimates, not verified production.
USGS-reported underground plans document the four mine levels and the long fourth-level workings.
Contemporary mining news described a 75-ton Venir Mining Company mill on Breece Hill.
A larger California Gulch milling plant was planned as an outgrowth of Venir milling operations; the small plant treated both mine and dump ore.
USGS surveyed and sampled the abandoned Venir mine-waste pile for environmental research.

moreHistory: USGS geologist Charles H. Behre documented the Venir, or South Ibex, shaft (L-59) on the west slope of Ball Mountain near Breece Hill, with four underground levels and intervening stopes. The mine worked northeast-trending gold-bearing quartz-pyrite veins in altered Johnson Gulch porphyry and operated intermittently from 1920 through 1935. The 1953 report gives approximate underground tunnel lengths of 3,180 feet on level one, 1,740 feet on level two, 430 feet on level three, and 6,210 feet on level four, but these are drift lengths rather than mine depth. Reported 1929 sampling indicated low-grade mineralization near the shaft; reserve figures were estimates, not confirmed mined output. Contemporary mining reports from 1940 described the Venir Mining Company's 75-ton milling plant on Breece Hill, led by John Cortellini with L. S. Harner as mill superintendent. A 1941 report described a proposed larger California Gulch mill arising from Venir operations; the small mill treated both mine and dump ore, so reported monthly tonnage cannot be attributed to Venir underground production alone. Decades later, USGS scientists surveyed and sampled the Venir waste pile for acid-rock drainage research. Nearby Ibex, Antioch, Sunday No. 2, and Garibaldi workings are distinct features.

sites.name: Vining Shaft
overview: The Vining was one of the mines that miners worked on Rock Hill during Leadville's silver-era boom. An 1881 account describes a shaft, a tunnel and a deeper winze as the Argent Mining Company explored the claim. By 1884 the operation had expanded into a major search for ore, but the richest material appeared in scattered pockets. Contemporary observers reported that the cost of prospecting kept the mine from paying consistently. Today its mapped location is approximate; the historical records do not verify an accessible shaft entrance.

timeline.text: Argent Mining Company worked the Vining claim near Rock and Dome; contemporary report described a shaft, tunnel and winze.
A contemporary account of Argent's property sale described a deep shaft and extensive prospecting on the Vining and adjacent Frank Shipman claims, with sporadic ore and poor profitability.
USGS Professional Paper 148 mapped and documented the geology of the Leadville district, including western Rock Hill workings.

moreHistory: In April 1881 the Engineering and Mining Journal reported that Argent had suspended work on its Chieftain claim and was developing the Vining claim near Rock and Dome mines. At that time a 60-foot shaft, 160-foot tunnel and 165-foot winze were reported. In September 1884, the Journal reported that Argent's properties, including Vining on Rock Hill and adjoining Frank Shipman, had been sold under a trust deed securing development debt contracted in 1881. It described a 350-foot shaft on the Vining/Frank Shipman properties, extensive underground prospecting, and irregular pockets of payable ore that kept the venture from consistent profitability. Manager Loomis was specifically named. USGS later included the western Rock Hill mines in its geological documentation. The Vining claim, Vining Shaft named feature, and adjacent Frank Shipman workings should not be conflated into one verified physical entrance.

sites.name: Vulture Mine
overview: Vulture Mine was a rich silver-and-lead working on Fryer Hill. Its story includes a shaft, a neighboring disputed claim, an 1880 mine fire, and an 1883 lease. Marker shows an approximate locality only.

timeline.text: Vulture supplied Leadville ore sampling operations; underground fire reported in its workings.
Original discoverer J. C. Langhorne leased southern Vulture ground.
USGS described Vulture No. 1 shaft and the lead-silver ore body.

moreHistory: USGS Emmons (1886) described Vulture No. 1 shaft opening a rich lead-silver ore body within the Chrysolite group. A nearby Triangle/Eaton claim was separate. In 1880 an underground fire affected Vulture workings; 1883 reporting identified original discoverer J. C. Langhorne as lessee of southern Vulture ground.

sites.name: White Cap Mine
overview: On Iron Hill east of Leadville, White Cap was part of a network of underground workings connected to the district's lead and silver mining era. A report from 1884 identifies its shaft as an ore-hoisting route for the Iron Hill Consolidated property. In 1901 a new lessee returned to the old shaft and pursued deeper mineralized ground, reaching a reported 712-foot station. Historic records document the workings, but the mine's exact entrance is not verified today.
moreHistory: In June 1884, contemporary mining reporting listed White Cap as one of Iron Hill Consolidated's claims leased on a royalty basis, amid pressure from falling lead prices. By September 1884, lessees Bunker and Kyle were working parts of the consolidated property, with ore from a north level hoisted through the White Cap shaft. In March 1901 the Nayr Mining Company leased the old White Cap Mine and adjoining Iron Hill ground, proposing to deepen its shaft to 760 feet in search of sulphide ore. By July 1901 a station was being cut at 712 feet in copper- and gold-bearing mineralized ground. Company-wide production or adjacent claims should not be misattributed to White Cap.

sites.name: Wilkesbarre Mine
overview: On a hillside above Shingle Mill Gulch, the Wilkesbarre Mine was driven toward a silver vein already worked from higher tunnels. The Arty and Snow vein was located in 1884, and the mining group later shipped silver-bearing ore. In 1924 miners worked on a lower tunnel intended to reach ore beneath the upper workings. Geologists mapped parts of this lower tunnel in 1951, preserving a detailed record of its fractured granite and vein geology. Historic reports frequently combine production from the upper and lower workings; the $15,000 reported for 1920–23 belongs to the upper Arty and Snow operation, not necessarily this portal. The map pin shows an approximate historic location; the entrance and land access are not verified.

timeline.text: The Arty and Snow silver vein was located; this was the vein later accessed by the Wilkesbarre mining group, not proof that the lower Wilkesbarre tunnel already existed.

Robert Morseman and associates drove more than 300 feet of adit on the Wilkesbarre group and encountered silver-bearing oxide ore; the precise attribution of this early drive to today's lower portal is uncertain.
The Wilkesbarre Mine shipped siliceous gold-silver ore.
Upper Arty and Snow workings yielded about $15,000 in gross production; this is group-level history, not proven production from the lower Wilkesbarre adit.
Workers developed a lower drift, probably today's Wilkesbarre adit #102, to intercept the Snow Lode vein beneath earlier upper workings.
USGS geologists could enter much of the lower Wilkesbarre adit and mapped its underground geology.
State mine inventories and subsequent Colorado Geological Survey research documented the Wilkesbarre adits and their waste-rock/environmental issues.

moreHistory: The Wilkesbarre mining group in the St. Kevin district developed the silver-bearing Arty and Snow vein. USGS reported that the vein was located in 1884, and that the lower Wilkesbarre portal lay in Shingle Mill Gulch, distinct from the upper Arty and Snow adit roughly 330 feet northeast. CGS archival research documents 1904 development of over 300 feet of group adit, 1910 siliceous gold-silver ore shipments, and lower-tunnel development in 1924 intended to intercept silver ore beneath the upper workings. Upper Arty/Snow workings shipped silver-bearing ore in the early 1920s; USGS valued their 1920-23 gross output at about $15,000, but this is not lower-adit-specific production. USGS geologists mapped accessible lower Wilkesbarre workings in 1951. CGS later inventoried the lower adit as #102 and noted waste-rock/environmental concerns. Historical records often combine the Wilkesbarre group and upper Arty/Snow production, so they must not be conflated with lower adit #102 or neighboring Griffin workings.

sites.name: Wolftone Mine
overview: The Wolftone Mine is one of Leadville’s especially story-rich historic workings: an 1876 discovery that evolved from early lead-silver development into an important zinc-era property. Its deep workings, unusual zinc minerals, and a documented 1911 underground banquet give the site both mining and social history beyond a simple mine identification.

timeline.text: Samuel Morgan and Aden Alexander located the Wolftone Mine on Carbonate Hill.
Malta Smelting and Mining Company requested survey; patent was granted later that year.
Ore was reported at 633 feet, including a seven-foot body of pyrite mixed with galena.
S. D. Nicholson searched old Wolftone workings for oxidized zinc and found a major zinc-silicate body.
A formal Robert Burns banquet was held underground at the Wolftone Mine.
The Wolftone shaft was reported at 1,120 feet deep with eight levels.

moreHistory: Located in 1876 by Samuel Morgan and Aden Alexander, the Wolftone began with five shallow shafts. Malta Smelting and Mining Company sought survey in 1880 and patent followed that year. By 1882 a deep shaft had encountered a seven-foot pyrite-galena body at 633 feet. The mine later joined the Adams and Maid of Erin as the A.M.W. properties under S. D. Nicholson. Around 1910 Nicholson searched old Wolftone workings after oxidized zinc became valuable and found what was described as the district’s largest body of zinc silicate. The mine became noted for zinc minerals and unusual mineralogy; by 1920 its shaft had reached about 1,120 feet with eight levels. A formal Robert Burns banquet was held underground at the Wolftone on January 25, 1911, documented by the Lake County Public Library historical collection.

sites.name: Yak Tunnel
overview: The Yak Tunnel was more than a hole through the mountain: it became underground infrastructure for an entire part of the Leadville mining district. Begun in the 1890s from the earlier Blow/Silver Cord project, it was extended for miles beneath Iron Hill and Breece Hill, draining flooded workings while also providing routes for exploration and ore haulage. Connections eventually reached major properties including the Resurrection mines. The same interconnected system that helped prolong mining later carried contaminated mine water toward California Gulch. That legacy made the Yak Tunnel a central part of the California Gulch Superfund cleanup, where it became Operable Unit 1 and mine water was captured and treated.

timeline.text: EPA and USGS records place the start of the Yak Tunnel drainage project in 1895, extending the earlier Silver Cord/Blow tunnel system.
Historical Leadville records report the Yak workings reached Resurrection No. 1.
EPA records state the final extension of the Yak Tunnel occurred in 1923.
The California Gulch mining area, including the Yak Tunnel, entered the federal Superfund program.
Yak Tunnel and its water-treatment facilities became California Gulch Operable Unit 1 for control and treatment of contaminated mine drainage.

moreHistory: The Yak Tunnel grew from the earlier Blow/Silver Cord tunnel project into one of the Leadville district’s most important pieces of underground infrastructure. EPA records state that it was driven beginning in 1895 as an extension of the Silver Cord Tunnel to drain the Iron Hill mines, then repeatedly extended through 1923. USGS describes the system as extending roughly 6.5 km east and northeast from its portal into some of the district’s most productive ground. Historical synthesis based on Leadville records documents the Yak Mining, Milling and Tunneling Company, the tunnel reaching the Resurrection No. 1 workings in 1908, further connections to Resurrection No. 2, and its use for drainage, ventilation and ore haulage. In the modern era the tunnel became a major environmental feature: EPA designated the Yak Tunnel and its treatment facilities as California Gulch Superfund Operable Unit 1, with remediation addressing metal-laden mine drainage.

sites.name: Yankee Doodle Mine
overview: On Leadville's Carbonate Hill, the Yankee Doodle grew from one of the district's early carbonate discoveries into a long-lived lead-silver producer. Historic reports trace deepening shafts, regular ore shipments, profitable operation under the Carbonate Hill Mining Company, and an 1897 sale after the mine had reportedly produced more than half a million dollars for its earlier owners.

timeline.text: Yankee Doodle was discovered during the wave of Carbonate Hill discoveries following the Carbonate Mine.
A new upper shaft was reported at 255 feet, still being sunk toward ore.
Yankee Doodle was listed among Carbonate Hill's producing mines, shipping about 60 tons per week.
Carbonate Hill Mining Company reported about $50,000 net profit from the mine through September 1.
The mine was sold to an Eastern syndicate for a reported price near $100,000 after reportedly yielding more than $500,000 to its old owners.

moreHistory: The Yankee Doodle was among the early carbonate discoveries that followed the 1877 Carbonate Mine discovery on Carbonate Hill. By 1880 the Carbonate Hill Mining Company was sinking a new upper shaft that had reached 255 feet, and later that year the mine was reported as markedly improved. January 1881 reporting listed Yankee Doodle among Carbonate Hill's producing mines. In 1882 the Carbonate Hill Mining Company confirmed ownership of the Yankee Doodle and reported roughly $50,000 net profit through September 1. Federal historical compilation reports steady production of about 175 to 200 tons of ore during a later year. In June 1897 the mine was sold to an Eastern syndicate for a reported price near $100,000; contemporary reporting described it as a major lead-carbonate producer that had already yielded more than $500,000 to its former owners.
